Beef, Hacks, Pluribus and The Pitt are a few of the TV shows nominated at this year's Emmy Awards, which take place on Monday in Los Angeles.
Widow's Bay, DTF St Louis, Slow Horses, The Bear and Abbott Elementary are also competing for prizes at the ceremony, which is seen as the US television industry's most prestigious event.
Actors nominated for trophies include Zendaya, Noah Wyle, Sarah Snook and Colman Domingo, while Matthew Rhys, Carey Mulligan and Jack Lowden are among the British nominees.
But several big shows are not represented - viral sensation Heated Rivalry is not eligible for the Emmys, while there is a weaker presence for the final series of Euphoria and Stranger Things.
Here's everything you need to know about this year's Emmy Awards.
Which TV shows are the frontrunners?
The Emmys split their nominations into three overarching categories: comedy, drama and limited or anthology series.
Best drama is generally seen as the night's most prestigious prize, and last year's winner The Pitt is back to defend its title following its second series.
The acclaimed medical drama also has eight individual acting nominations, including one for its star, Noah Wyle.
Other dramas nominated include Pluribus, Slow Horses, The Diplomat and Game of Thrones prequel A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms.
Over in the comedy categories, Hollywood satire Hacks is predicted by many to continue its hugely successful Emmys streak following its fifth and final season.
The show's expected wins could include acting prizes for its two stars, Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder.
Smart already has four Emmys for Hacks, having never lost for her performances in the previous four seasons. Another win would bring her total Emmy tally to eight, tying the record held by Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman.
Possible challengers in the comedy categories include Widow's Bay, Shrinking, Abbott Elementary and Nobody Wants This.
Elsewhere, the second season of Netflix's Beef could be a strong contender in the limited or anthology series category, and win acting prizes for its stars Carey Mulligan and Oscar Isaac.
But it faces strong competition from shows such as All Her Fault, The Beast in Me and DTF St Louis, which had a particularly strong showing at last week's Creative Arts Emmys.
British nominees alongside Mulligan include Riz Ahmed (Bait), Rufus Sewell (The Diplomat), Kate OâFlynn (Widowâs Bay) and Gary Oldman and Jack Lowden (both for Slow Horses).
And many are keeping a particularly close eye on Welsh star Matthew Rhys, who is nominated in two different lead actor categories - for comedy Widow's Bay and limited series The Beast in Me.
Why isn't Heated Rivalry nominated?
The buzziest show of the last year, Heated Rivalry, starring Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams, is missing from this year's Emmy nominations.
The ice hockey romance did not qualify because it is a fully financed Canadian production, without the US involvement needed to be recognised at the Emmys.
Its ineligibility puzzled many who remember Schitt's Creek, a show more Canadian than maple cream cookies, dominating the Emmys in 2021.
But that qualified because of its financial and broadcast partnerships in the US, including creator and star Dan Levy's own American-based production company.
Heated Rivalry will instead be eligible to compete for the next International Emmys, which take place in New York in November.
Meanwhile, two other viral shows popular with younger audiences that were eligible for the US ceremony had a weaker-than-expected showing in the nominations list.
The final series of Stranger Things is absent in the top categories this year, scoring only seven nominations in technical categories.
And despite its star-packed cast, Euphoria's last season managed only one acting nomination for former winner Zendaya.
What changes have been made to the ceremony?
Two categories have been merged this year - best talk series and best scripted variety series are now combined in a single category: outstanding variety series.
That means chat show hosts such as Jimmy Kimmel will compete against topical variety shows such as Saturday Night Live and Last Week Tonight With John Oliver.
Some other categories were also moved out of the telecast this year and have already been handed out, in an effort to revitalise the ceremony and leave more time for entertainment.
For example, best supporting actor and actress in a limited series, usually awarded during the main ceremony, were moved to the earlier Creative Arts Emmys ceremonies this year.
The total number of trophies awarded on the big night has been reduced from 26 to 19, a move the Academy said was intended to leave room for more musical performances, comedic sketches and unexpected acceptance speeches.
How to watch the Emmy Awards
The ceremony will begin at 17:00 PT / 20:00 ET on Monday, taking place at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
US viewers can watch the Emmy Awards live on NBC or on streaming service Peacock.
In the UK, it will start at 01:00 BST on Tuesday morning, but no British broadcaster is scheduled to show it live.
However, there will be overnight coverage on the BBC News website throughout the red carpet and ceremony.
Who has already won?
Winners at last weekend's Creative Arts Emmys included DTF St Louis stars Linda Cardellini and David Harbour, who won best supporting actress and actor in a limited series.
Betty Gilpin (Widow's Bay), Ernest Harden Jr (The Pitt), Shailene Woodley (Paradise) and the late Rob Reiner (The Bear) all won prizes for their guest acting roles, while British star Julie Andrews won best voiceover performance for Bridgerton.
Other British winners included Alan Cumming, who won best reality host for the US version of The Traitors.
Remarkably Bright Creatures, a drama starring Sally Field and Lewis Pullman about a perceptive octopus who observes the staff in his aquarium, won best movie.
South Park won best animated series, Mr. Scorsese took best docuse

It's been a little over 18 months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country's relationship with the United States, based on over a century of tight economic and military cooperation, was "over".
Trade talks collapsing, tit-for-tat tariffs, and Donald Trump's talk of making Canada a "51st state" have all fuelled this bitter feud between the two North American neighbours.
Now, as Canada's top pitch man, Carney is looking to leverage personal relationships from his time spent in the top tiers of global finance to woo some of the world's wealthiest asset managers and business leaders to bet on his country.
For two days, Toronto will host more than 100 global investors overseeing more than C$100tn ($72tn; Â£53) in assets, in the hope that new economic relationships will help Canada navigate an increasingly unstable geopolitical climate.
"Canada has what the world wants," said Carney ahead of this "first of its kind" investment summit.
On Monday and Tuesday, a luxury hotel will host guests from major sovereign wealth funds from around the world - including the United Arab Emirates and Norway - and chief executives from major finance companies, like BlackRock's Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.
There, Carney hopes to pitch them on Canada's energy and resource sectors, as well as the countryâs political stability, in the hopes of getting them to invest in AI, defence, transportation, and infrastructure projects across the country.
It is all part of a strategy to build a "more independent, more resilient economy" in Canada in the wake of the tariff war with the US, which has escalated in recent weeks.
But there is no guarantee that the deep-pocketed investors will be easily sold, and challenges include a track record in Canada of lengthy approvals for projects.
A recent report by the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, which will co-host the summit, cautioned that the scale and depth of investible opportunity is the country's greatest weakness.
"Global capital is looking for opportunity, but opportunity alone does not make a market investible," said Naomi Powell, director of the CPP Investments Insight Institute.
While shifting away from its closest business partner will prove a test for Carney, the former central banker has an address book full of the world's biggest business bosses and is on first-name terms with many of them.
"These were personal invites in many cases, literally," said Goldy Hyder, president and chief executive of the Business Council of Canada.
"It's not a group of politicians inviting financiers, it's a group of former financiers and investment people inviting their former buddies," added Miville Tremblay, who worked with Carney for several years at the Bank of Canada, and saw his skills on show during the 2008 global financial crisis.
"He was way above everyone," he said. "He understands finance very deeply. [He] would know when they are bluffing and when the understatement meant that something really bad was happening."
Knowing the minds of investors gives the prime minister, who began his career at investment bank Goldman Sachs, an advantage this week.
Carney is betting his background will boost his country's economic future, though there's little doubt that Canada stands to lose the most from any permanent divorce with the US, the world's largest economy.
Tremblay said Canada seeking investment from overseas was not new, but that the selling pitch to large corporations had now changed.
For the past 25 years, Canada's trade ministers used its proximity to the US as a selling point, pitching to foreign investors that they should "invest in Canada because you've got an easy access to the US market", Tremblay said.
"This line doesn't work anymore."
While the US-Canada trade war rumbles on, many believe there will come a moment when both sides return to the negotiating table.
Bradley Saunders, North America economist for Capital Economics, said securing the future of the trade deal was the "really important thing" for Carney to achieve in the longer term.
"Trade exports to the US are worth 20% of Canada's GDP - that's one of the highest rates in terms of bilateral trade between any two countries in the world.
"If Carney wants to attract long-term investment... he wants this to go well, he has to try and provide a stable environment - and that won't come until Canada has a certain trading relationship with the US."
Tremblay added even if Canada cut its trade with the US over the longer term, it was clear "they'll have to sit down and make a compromise".
Hyder cautioned that investors will want Carney to prove he can fix other barriers to investment, including ensuring indigenous communities and provinces - who have the power to slow or kill major resource projects - are on board with proposals.
Tremblay said the pitch has to be "Canada has stuff that the world needs" - which is the exact phrasing Carney has opted for.
Unless a deal was already in the works with another nation, however, he believes it's unlikely any big announcements will be made. He said while overseas investment will be a main aim, encouraging more domestic investment from Canada's largest pension funds, which currently invest more overseas, is also important.
Tremblay added the current tumultuous economic and political climate is perfect for his former boss. "He's a crisis manager. He managed the financial crisis, he managed Brexit, and now he's got a super crisis for Canada."
Carney has been clear that the road ahead for Canada as it pivots away from its reliance on the US will be a tough one.
So far, the majority of Canadians support his course of action, despite some criticism he is turning away from climate commitments as well as towards closer ties with nations like Saudi Arabia and China, as he pushes Canada's rich resources.

Alexander Zverev used his greater experience to beat home hope Ben Shelton in the US Open final and quiet a partisan crowd hoping to laud a rare American men's champion.
German top seed Zverev lifted a heavy burden by winning his first major title at this year's French Open and has quickly added another with a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory over Shelton in New York.
At the start of the season, there were question marks over whether 29-year-old Zverev would ever win one of the sport's most prestigious prizes.
Now he is celebrating becoming a multiple Grand Slam singles champion, having seen the path to glory partially cleared by injuries to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.
Sinner and Alcaraz swept the board between them at the majors in 2024 and 2025 - and Zverev has taken full advantage against the rest of the field in their absences.
Big-hitting Shelton, 23, has long been identified as a player who can win the biggest titles, but ultimately came up short in his first Grand Slam final against a rejuvenated Zverev.
Eighth seed Shelton was aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick in 2003, but losing serve in the first game of the match set the tone as Zverev controlled the opening two sets.
The momentum shifted in the third set, however, as Shelton finally started applying serious pressure on Zverev's serve.
Taking his third break opportunity provided encouragement to the 24,000 home fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium, but starting the fourth set with a poor service game allowed Zverev to reassert his authority and extinguish American dreams.
Zverev did not initially know he had secured victory when Shelton hit a return long on championship point, only breaking out into a broad and slightly surprised smile after his team pointed out the score to him.
Zverev uses Grand Slam-winning experience to see off Shelton
Going into the 2026 season, few people would have backed Zverev to win two Grand Slam tournaments, with the German having already lost three major finals in a career which looked in danger of not living up to expectation.
But injuries to his biggest rivals - Alcaraz missing the French Open and Wimbledon, with Sinner ruled out of the US Open - opened the door for Zverev.
A below-par Zverev scraped through the opening rounds at Flushing Meadows in a series of early-morning finishes, but he gradually improved over a fortnight where he did not play a top-20 opponent until Shelton.
Zverev had not lost to Shelton in their five previous meetings and immediately capitalised on a nervy start by his opponent.
Shelton double-faulted on break point in the first game of the match, handing over the type of initiative that opponents often struggle to wrestle back from Zverev.
Through the strength of his first serve, and his ability to unpick Shelton's weaker backhand in the baseline exchanges, Zverev rolled through the opening set and clinched it when Shelton hit another double fault on set point.
Zverev continued to patiently draw mistakes from Shelton in the second set, but without being gifted a break when his only opportunity arrived in the fourth game.
He instead showed why he has a strong tie-break record with another nerveless display and, unlike in the 2020 US Open final when he lost from a two-set lead, kept his composure in the pressure moments to secure a commanding victory.
Addressing his team which is led by his father Alexander senior and brother Mischa, Zverev said: "We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now won two in the span of three months.
"I think God has seen how hard we have worked, how hard we have suffered and how much pain we went through.
"I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."
Positives for Shelton - but work still to do
Despite the bitter disappointment of losing Sunday's showpiece, Shelton will take pride from his run to a first major final, as well as further belief he can win a Grand Slam title.
Shelton came into the tournament with confidence after winning the Canadian Open last month, but also with a point to prove after an underwhelming season at the Grand Slams.
A chastening first-round exit at Wimbledon against Finnish qualifier Otto Virtanen was described by Shelton as "one of the toughest losses" of his career, acting as a wake-up call going into the North American hard court swing.
He has bounced back superbly to come close to ending America's 23-year wait for somebody to finally follow in Roddick's footsteps.
Shelton did not have an easy route to the final, needing to overcome a series of big-hitting opponents which included three former top-10 players as well as seven-time major champion Alcaraz.
Shelton had never beaten a top-three opponent until powering past Alcaraz - who was playing in his first tournament for almost five months - in an epic quarter-final which ended at 3:34am.
However, he could not double that tally against world number two Zverev.
Shelton's recent success has been a product of developing his defensive skills and improving his weaker backhand, but not being able to execute his damaging forehand in crucial moments against Zverev proved costly.
It was a reminder of the work the American number one still has to do at the highest level against the very best opponents.
"I'm excited with the progress that I feel that I've made, but this one stings 100%," said Shelton.
"I made too many errors when I had the ball there on my strings."

0f558b4b28ce.text: The biggest surprise of last week's Republican midterm convention began with an audacious request from the organizers to GOP Sen. Dave McCormick: Could he get Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, a fellow Pennsylvanian, to make an appearance? "I'll ask him," McCormick said. Within days, Fetterman — who's been increasingly at odds with the Democratic Party's liberal wing — was on board. Why it matters: Fetterman's 64-second video — calling himself a "common-sense Democrat," praising McCormick and vowing to work with President Trump to defend Pennsylvania's steel industry — represented Fetterman's biggest break yet with his party. Behind the scenes: According to three sources familiar with the talks, the idea for Fetterman to make the appearance emerged over the summer, as organizers of the Dallas convention sought what they called an "Oh sh*t" moment. They were looking to drive home a key midterm message — that Democrats are too extreme. Organizers discussed featuring "walk away" figures — people who had supported Democrats but had become disillusioned with the party. Republican operative Tony Sayegh, a leading convention organizer, was a driving force behind the idea, and Trump adviser Jason Miller backed the plan. Fetterman topped their list. Zoom in: Sayegh, a friend of McCormick's, took the idea to him in July. McCormick had developed a friendship with Fetterman as the Democrat grew more estranged from his party, particularly over many Democrats' criticism of Israel. Organizers knew getting Fetterman involved would be a massive coup. The intrigue: McCormick approached Fetterman carefully, knowing the backlash his Democratic colleague could face if he agreed to a role in the GOP convention. McCormick asked Fetterman to introduce him at the convention. A source said McCormick added: "I don't want you to do something that's not good for you." The two senators hashed it out over calls and texts for a few days. "I want to do it. I'm sure it will make people mad," Fetterman told McCormick, according to the source. "But you're my friend, and I want to introduce you." Fetterman's decision was driven by his friendship with McCormick, not a desire to help Republicans , said a source familiar with his thinking. Fetterman "had no interest in being a pawn in a larger Republican play," the source said. There was brief talk of Fetterman traveling to Dallas to introduce McCormick in person, but he decided against it. Instead, Fetterman proposed recording a video outside a steel mill near his home in Braddock, Pa. McCormick's team arranged for a videographer to meet him there. Fetterman didn't use a script. He riffed in front of the camera. He focused on introducing McCormick and highlighting their bipartisan work in support of Pennsylvania's steel industry. Neither McCormick nor convention organizers tried to alter what he said. The notion of Fetterman switching parties never came up, according to a source familiar with the deliberations. Organizers saw Fetterman's appearance as a jolt that would draw eyeballs to the first-of-its-kind midterm convention — and play big on social media. To preserve the surprise, organizers kept the circle tight. McCormick looped in his chief of staff, Mark Isakowitz, and only a few others. Miller was Sayegh's point of contact in the White House. Fetterman went even further: He told no one on his team, a source told Axios. The bottom line: Fetterman's appearance at Trump's convention deepened his estrangement from the Democratic Party. But Fetterman reiterated after his appearance that he isn't switching parties, calling himself a "lifelong Democrat" and saying that if Democrats win control of the Senate in November, he'd remain the "51st vote."

The little girl stared up at Norma Gómez from the doorway of her neighbor’s apartment, her sad, brown eyes suddenly flashing with hope.
“Are you the person who’s going to bring my mom back?” she asked.
Gómez struggled to find an answer. It was a December morning, and she’d brought food, diapers, baby wipes, and clothes — items she hoped would help the 6-year-old girl, her baby brother, and the neighbor who had stepped in to care for them. The children were left alone after federal immigration agents arrested their parents outside their apartment in Oxnard, a mostly Latino agricultural community on the Southern California coast. But Gómez had no power to bring the parents back.
“We’re working on that,” Gómez recalled telling the girl. In reality, she was at a loss for how to answer truthfully without upsetting her.
As a project manager for a nonprofit that provides food assistance to immigrant families affected by Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, Gómez has witnessed the tumult and pain that have roiled the lives of millions of immigrant families since President Donald Trump returned to office, with devastating consequences for children’s health. They include an estimated 205,000 children with at least one parent detained by immigration authorities through April, a number that has undoubtedly climbed since. Separation from parents harms children psychologically. It destabilizes families, often leaving the remaining parent or caregiver scrambling to stay housed, buy food, and fulfill kids’ medical needs. Some kids are left alone to care for themselves.
Many kids whose parents aren’t detained are experiencing threats to their health and well-being too. Two children in the South died by suicide in February 2025 after reportedly being bullied over their family’s alleged immigration status.
Millions of children live in families losing access to medical care, food, tax credits, and other supports as federal and state governments roll back eligibility for immigrants with and without legal status. Fear of federal enforcement has pushed parents to avoid taking kids to school, going to the doctor, and engaging in social activities. Some have disenrolled from or avoided signing kids up for health and nutrition programs.
Children from immigrant backgrounds are also living in fear. They’re experiencing more emotional distress, increased bullying in school, and anxiety about racial profiling by ICE, even when they or their family members are citizens or legal residents.
Most of these children are American citizens. About 1 in 4 U.S.-born kids have an immigrant parent, including around 4.6 million with a parent who lacks legal status.
“I’m really concerned about how long it’s going to take for us as a country to address all of the harm that’s happening to this generation of kids,” said Wendy Cervantes, director of immigration and immigrant families at the Center for Law and Social Policy. “This type of stress can have long-term developmental harm and can really inhibit their ability to do well in school, to have good health outcomes, and to grow into thriving, stable adults.”
Curbing Public Benefits
Trump has made cracking down on immigrants — including the children of immigrants — a priority since his second term began last year. On Inauguration Day, he issued an executive order purporting to end birthright citizenship for kids born to parents without legal status or in the country on temporary visas, an attempt ultimately blocked by the Supreme Court.
His administration, with the approval of Republicans in Congress, has poured billions of dollars into immigration enforcement, detaining the parents of an estimated 145,000 U.S. citizen children as of April, and, according to an analysis by nonprofit newsroom The Marshall Project, over 6,200 children. It’s sought to rescind temporary protected status, or TPS, for over 1 million immigrants, tens of thousands of whom have U.S. citizen children, and stalled renewals in the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which includes the parents of about 300,000 citizen children.
White House officials say the immigration crackdown benefits American citizens by freeing up resources such as jobs and housing, reducing pressure on public coffers, expelling criminals, and restoring integrity to the immigration system. (Studies have shown that mass deportations harm U.S. workers.) Trump and other Republican leaders have argued that birthright citizenship encourages unauthorized immigration and “birth tourism,” and that TPS has allowed immigrants from “dangerous, third-world countries” to remain in the United States indefinitely under what is supposed to be a temporary program.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis did not directly address whether the administration is concerned about long-term harm to children and increased healthcare costs because of its immigration policies. Instead, she repeated past White House criticisms that President Joe Biden’s immigration policies allowed children to be trafficked across the U.S. border.
“The real story is the psychiatric impact on the tens of thousands of children who were smuggled across the border — many by human and sex traffickers,” she wrote in an email.
Only 39% of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of immigration, according to a recent Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
Stephen Miller, the chief architect of Trump’s immigration policies, has accused the children of immigrants of draining public resources and perpetuating problems from their parents’ home countries. Research, however, shows that immigrants earn more and do better the longer they live in the United States and that they and their children assimilate rapidly. Data also shows they rely less on welfare than native-born Americans.

On the night of July 6, a storm moved over northern Minnesota near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. The boreal forest there, composed of species like balsam fir, spruce and pine, was extremely dry after a flash drought and unusually warm temperatures sapped the trees of their moisture.
As the storm blew across the sky, rain didn’t even reach the ground. Many of the 700 lightning strikes did.
“Coniferous boreal forest is one of the most flammable vegetation types on the planet,” said Lee Frelich, director of the University of Minnesota Center for Forest Ecology. “It just exploded into fire with those ignitions.”
The flames raged for two months, eventually scorching 64,000 acres of northern Minnesota’s forest. Some are still smoldering. Further north, fires burned even more land in Canada’s boreal forest, consuming 730,000 acres in what people called the 300-mile wall of fire.
“The Western U.S. has always been notorious for wildfires,” said Eric Evenson, a meteorologist and science communications specialist at the North Atlantic Fire Science Exchange. “However, we’re seeing it flaring up in other parts of the country due to these extremes as the climate changes.”
Human-caused global warming is amping up extreme weather conditions that led to this summer’s Minnesota and Canadian fires. Fires in the boreal forest happen more often, and when they do, they burn more acreage than they did in the late 20th century, an accelerating pattern that picked up even more speed in the past five years.
Trends are clear in Canada, where there is more forested land. But the same could happen in Minnesota and other areas of the Midwest as climate change alters forest types and conditions. Nearly 91 million acres of forest covers swaths of the Midwest, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
Researchers and government climate reports expect wildfire risk to increase in Midwestern forests. Multiple changes feed into that: Warmer conditions stretch across more months of the year. Temperatures climb ever higher. Stronger storms release more rain over shorter periods of time, spurring plant growth, but sudden droughts occur more often as well, drying out the plants to provide more fuel for fire. The swing from one condition to the other now has a name: hydroclimate whiplash. More lightning streaks across the sky and electrifies the ground thanks to a warmer atmosphere that holds more moisture and strengthens storms, which often blow down trees, material susceptible to burning.
“The definition of fire season is something that’s shifting,” said Julia DeFeo, a forest and fire ecologist at Ohio State University. “We more often have the conditions that are conducive to wildfire outside of what would historically have been considered the normal timeframes.”
Changing Forests
Before colonization in Minnesota and parts of Wisconsin and Michigan, Indigenous people managed the coniferous forests with fire. Tree ring data from 1600 on, information cataloged by a Minnesota fire ecologist and kept up to date, show burns during wet years when they were less likely to get out of control.
When Europeans settled the region, they cut down large sections of forest, created fire exclusion zones and suppressed fire. Aspen and birch, two tree species that hold more moisture, grew in place of the conifers, leading to an abnormally low amount of fire. In the 1990s, more flammable conifers began to replace the aspen and birch as part of the forest’s natural succession, and the number of fires increased again.
“We’ve returned to what I view as a normal fire frequency in northern Minnesota,” said Frelich. “Now the question is, will that continue to increase and go beyond the historical normal because of climate change?”
The story is a bit different further south in Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio. Deciduous trees such as red oak, hemlock and beech grew more abundantly there. But without fire, red maples encroached, slowly taking over the oak forests around the mid-19th century. Unlike oaks, whose leaves curl and aerate the ground, maples’ flat leaves lock in moisture when they fall and make the ground wetter and harder to ignite.
Hotter, arid conditions could change that.
“When things do get sufficiently dry,” said DeFeo, “then it’s a tinderbox.”
A History of Infernos
Though people don’t historically think of the Midwest as a wildfire hotspot, two of the largest conflagrations in U.S. history occurred in the region. In October 1871, it was gripped by drought. Logging companies in northeastern Wisconsin near a town called Peshtigo left branches and felled trees on the land, and farmers clearing properties to grow crops burned debris. When winds gusted through the area, fire quickly spread, scorching 1.2 million acres and killing hundreds, if not thousands, of people.
At the same time, the Great Chicago Fire overtook the city, killing 300 people and turning buildings to ash. Other fires collectively known as the Great Michigan Fire occurred on the same night, incinerating 2.5 million acres.
It’s unlikely that a similar situation would occur today. Drought and fuel monitoring and newer communication technologies keep us better informed about potential threats, said Evenson. Yet fire managers see the need to mitigate risk by building with fire-safe materials and identifying vulnerable structures where human development meets or intermingles with unoccupied areas covered with vegetation, spaces known as the wildland-urban interface.

A Malaysian teenage boy charged with the high-profile murder of a female schoolmate has been acquitted, with the judge finding the boy was mentally unsound during the incident.
He had fatally stabbed Yap Shing Xuen in a toilet at their secondary school on the outskirts of the capital Kuala Lumpur.
The killing of the 16-year-old girl had shocked Malaysia and sparked debate about the effects of social media on children.
Police previously had said they suspected social media could have influenced the boy, who was 14 at the time. The case was seen to have spurred authorities to limit children's access to social media, which began earlier this year.
The boy - who cannot be named under Malaysian law as he is still a minor - had pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
During the trial defence lawyers did not deny that the boy killed the girl, but argued that he had suffered from poor mental health for years and asked for his acquittal on the grounds of insanity.
An expert witness, a psychiatrist, testified that the boy had schizophrenia, and had suffered from mental illness and experienced delusions since he was nine years old.
The boy's condition was said to have worsened during the pandemic and when he eventually returned to school. Lawyers had said that the boy would need medication for the rest of his life to manage symptoms.
On Monday the judge ruled that the boy would be acquitted, but also ordered for him to be detained and to receive treatment at a psychiatric hospital.
He will stay at the hospital until he is deemed fit to be released back to society, and would likely be subject to yearly assessments.
A defence lawyer told reporters on Monday that upon hearing the verdict, the boy appeared "neutral in emotion, but he understands what is going on, [that] it's a very serious matter".
The trial and verdict hearings were held in a closed court, which meant that the public and media could not attend.
The case has profoundly shocked Malaysia and sparked a nationwide conversation about the negative effects of social media on children.
Much of this conversation was triggered by the contents of a note that police had found on the boy at the time of his arrest, which was leaked online and widely circulated.
Some people had compared the case to the Netflix series Adolescence, which featured a storyline about a young boy killing a female schoolmate and explored the theme of online radicalisation.
Last year, the country's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was asked about the case as well as other recent cases of violence in schools.
He was quoted by local media as saying that "almost all of these issues stem from the use of mobile phones and social media", and vowed to look into stricter measures.
Authorities have since put in place new rules which they say will protect children and reduce their exposure to harmful online content.
Since June, Malaysia has banned all children under the age of 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms.
Additional reporting by Diyana Nawwar

Before Iowa was the nation’s most wind-powered state, it generated nearly all of its electricity with coal. Since 2000, the fossil fuel’s role in the state’s power mix has diminished as utilities built a massive fleet of wind turbines that now provides nearly two-thirds of the state’s power.
But as the artificial intelligence boom drives up electricity demand and utility-scale wind and solar development slows, coal has helped make up lost ground.
From 2024 to 2025, Iowa’s two largest electric utilities both increased their generation of coal power for the first time in years, according to the Iowa Environmental Council’s annual report on statewide electricity generation, which draws on data reported to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
In 2024, coal made up 21 percent of the resource mix of MidAmerican Energy Co., the largest investor-owned electric utility in Iowa. In 2025, it supplied 27 percent of the company’s total power. Interstate Power and Light, a subsidiary of Alliant Energy Corp., reported coal jumping from 12 to 20 percent of its mix in the same timeline.
“It’s confusing, frankly,” Steve Guyer, senior energy policy counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council, said of the uptick. Emissions monitoring data submitted to the Environmental Protection Agency by Iowa’s six coal plants suggest that the trend has continued in 2026, he said.
Iowa is home to a small, aging coal fleet made up of just nine utility-scale generating plants. The dated facilities are significant sources of nitrogen and sulfur oxide gases, toxic heavy metals—like mercury and carcinogenic arsenic and cadmium—and fine particulate matter that exacerbates asthma and underlying lung and heart disease, said Peter Thorne, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa. “They really reflect a turn-of-the-19th-century technology,” he said.
With the long-term decline in coal generation, Iowa’s remaining plants have operated at “incredibly low capacity,” around 20 percent, for many years, said Josh Mandelbaum, an Iowa-based senior attorney with the Environmental Law and Policy Center who was not involved with the report. “In a period of rising demand, where the lower-cost clean resources aren’t getting built out as much as they should be, or as quickly as they should be, that’s when you’ll see something like coal fill the gap,” Mandelbaum said.
Iowa’s electricity generation increased from 70.5 million megawatt-hours in 2024 to just over 74 million in 2025. The Iowa Nuclear Energy Task Force, convened this year by Gov. Kim Reynolds, has attributed the growth in electricity demand to data center development and the expansion of manufacturing facilities.
The rising demand coincides with an already fraught period for utility-scale renewables. Large-scale wind and solar projects must contend with the loss of federal tax credits, growing opposition from residents and rising materials costs due to tariffs, Mandelbaum said.
The Iowa Environmental Council’s report documented noticeable impacts to air quality from just one year of increased coal combustion. From 2024 to 2025, Alliant and MidAmerican reported a more than 50 percent increase in their emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, according to data filed with the EPA.
In the atmosphere, those gases can react to form additional fine particulate matter, particles half the size of a red blood cell that play havoc in the body. As coal emissions rose, the council found, government-run air quality monitoring locations in the state saw a corresponding increase in particulate matter concentrations.
Air pollution is increasingly recognized as a significant contributor to cancer risk, Guyer noted. Cancer is top of mind in Iowa, the state with the second-highest rate of new cancer cases, a share that continues to grow.
In response to a request for comment, Alliant Energy wrote that the utility “remains focused on our commitment to balancing reliability, affordability and sustainability for customers, while making progress toward our goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.”
MidAmerican also advertises a net-zero goal by 2050.
“One important point is sometimes lost in discussions about Iowa’s energy future: how much progress has already occurred,” wrote Geoff Greenwood, MidAmerican’s media relations manager, in an email to Inside Climate News. Since 2005, the utility has nearly doubled its total electricity generation but has reduced carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 30 percent, and both nitrogen oxide and sulfur oxide emissions by over 70 percent, Greenwood wrote.
Greenwood also pointed to the importance of coal generation in ensuring reliable service to MidAmerican’s 1.3 million electric customers in Iowa. “In years when wind output is lower, other generating resources must provide the electricity customers depend on,” he wrote.
Reliability is often cited as a shortcoming of renewable energy sources that depend on naturally variable wind and sunlight. However, advanced energy-storage infrastructure could help affordably meet demand without turning to coal, Thorne said. During periods of high wind and solar production, Iowa could use excess electricity to produce hydrogen for later use, or pump water to reservoirs upstream, creating stored energy that could be harnessed as hydroelectric power when demand spikes.
The uptick in coal generation over the past two years reflects rising energy demand and delays in implementing cleaner technologies, said Mandelbaum. “I don’t think it signifies a trend for coal. I think it signifies that cheaper alternatives are not being built quickly enough,” he said. “It will continue to be a problem until we get the fleet retired.”

As the Federal Reserve weighs whether to raise interest rates this week, Chair Kevin Warsh must choose between breaking marketsâ trust and triggering President Donald Trumpâs ire.
Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently joined the president in arguing for lower interest rates. But investors overwhelmingly expect Warsh to deliver on his hawkish speech in Jackson Hole last month.

House Democrats are circulating a letter imploring President Donald Trump to lead an international effort to set global AI rules, according to a copy shared with Semafor.
âWe strongly urge your administration to lead a coordinated international effort to establish a global framework to guide the development of this technology and a shared vision for AI end-use â engaging our strongest allies, such as the European Union, as well as formidable global competitors, particularly the Peopleâs Republic of China,â Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., writes in the draft of the letter to be sent later this week.
Itâs unclear which other lawmakers will sign on.
The push precedes President Donald Trumpâs meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, which will touch on AI.
Panic over AIâs capabilities is also rising among lawmakers and the American public.
âWe must lead with the creation of global rules of the road to prevent the proliferation of uncontrollable highly capable frontier AI,â the letter reads, comparing the push to past US-led efforts on nuclear power and aviation.
The US has been very clear about its desire to lead China in AI development, and itâs unlikely that the Trump administration would play any role in international policy decisions about AI that would involve ceding competitive ground. On Sunday, Trump rejected calls by tech leaders for a slowdown in AI development, citing the need for the US to outcompete China.
The White House has often opted out of global discussions about AI; last year, White House science adviser Michael Kratsios said at the UN: âWe totally reject all efforts by international bodies to assert centralized control and global governance of AI.â
Itâs still possible the rapid pace of AI development will shift the administrationâs approach. Trumpâs talks with Xi on AI, and the upcoming UN General Assembly, will present a chance to test whether his administration has altered course at all.

The News
Some Republicans are hoping they can address votersâ affordability concerns before the election â potentially by passing a data center power bill to demonstrate the party is listening to souring popular sentiment surrounding AI infrastructure.
The House is set to take up the bill, called the Ratepayer Protection Act, this week, which will help vulnerable incumbents answer votersâ concerns about data centers. If the Senate takes it up, the bill would help endangered Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio.
But the body has other priorities: The Senate is scheduled to take up the crypto market structure bill and a huge bipartisan college sports bill as soon as this week.
Thereâs a faction of Republicans whoâd rather concentrate on deregulatory rollbacks and addressing AIâs impact on utility bills; Republicans will try and sort it out this week in party meetings.
Know More
Most Senate denizens expect Tuesdayâs crypto bill to fail given the standoff over new ethics rules governing President Donald Trump and his family. The Protect College Sports Act has better prospects and could receive a vote as early as this week.
Members of both parties are optimistic about the college sports bill despite Democratsâ filibuster leverage, and one of the billâs wealthy benefactors is trying to make sure it stays front and center. Saving College Sports, a group founded by Texas Tech University System Board of Regents Chair Cody Campbell, is spending an additional $300,000 on ads between Monday and Tuesday on programs watched closely by lawmakers, including on Fox News, MS NOW and CNN, according to a person familiar with the plans.
If the bill advances on the Senate floor, it could take a significant amount of time to process â especially if thereâs a protracted amendment fight. That would threaten to eat into the limited three-week work session before the midterm elections, limiting other legislative action; Senate Republicans also wanted to confirm Trumpâs judicial nominees and Keith Sonderling, his new pick for Labor secretary.
Senate Republicans are also coordinating with the House about deregulatory rollbacks they might be able to accomplish this month. The House is scheduled to take up two California environmental disapproval resolutions this week â membersâ last week in town before they break ahead of the midterms.
By taking the lead on the data center power bill, House Republicans could provide some political cover for that billâs sponsor, purple-district Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo.
The House is also set to vote on a Senate-passed bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., that would ratchet up pressure on Russia by penalizing its trading partners, though many House Democrats are expected to oppose it because of concerns about handing over more tariff authority to Trump.

The sudden appearance of alignment among AI CEOs about industry regulation over the weekend masks an inconvenient reality for Congress: There is no consensus.
In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson is downplaying his own role in favor of a âpartnershipâ with AI companies, as he told CNN on Sunday.
Across the Capitol, OpenAI remains most supportive of bipartisan Senate Commerce Committee talks that could advance this week, despite skepticism from Anthropic, Democrats, and AI safety groups, who say those negotiations risk letting the industry self-police.
But Saturdayâs three-CEO agreement that frontier models are accelerating too fast centered on Anthropicâs plan to do âthings every AI lab needs to do anyway,â as our colleague Reed Albergotti wrote â which amounts to self-regulation, with labs likely choosing their own independent evaluators.
âThe time to act is now, before itâs too late,â Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., told Semafor.
She urged Johnson to keep the House in session past this week to work on AI, but her own leader is already looking to 2027.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told ABC on Sunday that his caucus would gather this week to discuss options.
At a separate closed-door fireside chat with Jeffries last week, former President Barack Obama urged the New Yorker to âput together a framework for a very public conversationâ and said heâd prioritize the issue if he were running for president, according to excerpts of the remarks confirmed by Obamaâs office.

b0c6eb22f432.text:
Lockheed’s Skunk Works plans to build four more of its multirole combat drones
The firm’s top secret research arm shared new Vectis images, but few key details.
Skunk Works, Lockheed Martin’s secretive research arm, plans to build four more of its experimental, multipurpose drones as the firm attempts to sell its futuristic platform to the U.S. military.
Last year, Skunk Works unveiled Vectis—a concept for a group 5 drone that’s capable of a wide range of missions. Now, on the first day of the Air & Space Force Association’s defense conference near Washington, D.C., company officials announced they’re making significant progress on the prototype and are already planning to expand the fleet for more tests.
“We are moving forward with a plan to build an additional four vehicles, bringing a total of five to include the original prototype,” said Ron Fehlen, Skunk Works’ vice president and general manager. “Development work on those additional aircraft is already underway, and we'll have more specifics to share soon.”
Company officials shared new images of the Skunk Works combat drone with reporters ahead of this week’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference. Vectis will be roughly 34 feet long and have a 38-foot wingspan, and will feature a submerged engine inlet and a tail-less body to reduce drag and mission flexibility,” Fehlen said. While Lockheed was eager to talk about the aircraft’s design, the Skunk Works vice president was tight-lipped about who the specific customer for the new aircraft could be, and didn’t provide details on the weapons loadout, propulsion system, or estimated cost of the platform. The Air Force, Marine Corps, and Navy are all aiming to field collaborative combat aircraft.
“From an affordability standpoint, which we're always looking at, and, of course, are targeting to be the CCA competitive price. So we're very cognizant of it and make trades associated with that, Fehlen said. “It's obviously, I think, focused more on the CCA side of the house, and obviously the price points that are highly relevant in that regime.”
Fehlen said the company remains on track to fly Vectis by “the end of 2027.” He said Skunk Works feels confident in that timeline, due in part, to the use of digital designs and “minimal tooling determinant assembly”—which the Skunk Works vice president likened to ready-to-assemble furniture with pre-drilled holes.
“It's a technique that really enables an increased level of affordability and speed through really reducing the amount of touch labor required and increasing the first pass yield,” Fehlen said. “We've seen in many cases an 80 percent reduction in labor hours to build up the aircraft itself.”
While Fehlen wouldn’t specify one specific U.S. program or customer Vectis is geared toward, he did say it could work with any of Lockheed Martin’s fighter jets, which are also flown by other nation’s militaries.
“I'll point to the fact that we have a long history in crewed tactical systems that, you know, Vectus is going to need to integrate with, in addition to other fighter aircraft that are produced around the world,” Fehlen said. “So, from our perspective, this is in line with our heritage and what we're producing today and delivering to the field. It has incredible capability, and now we're going to be able to add this to it.”

b89db9283116.text: President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain. Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down. Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress. Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1 , applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China. Speaking in Ireland on Sunday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins." It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or " pace the frontier " — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations. David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer : Slow yourselves down. If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium. Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand. His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said Sunday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety. The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency, but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet Tuesday to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority. The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for. On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison . Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews. What to watch: The unprecedented push for restraint from inside the AI industry, colliding with deepening public unease, could scramble this political stalemate. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a Trump ally running in a swing state, said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's new warning convinced him "we must slow down development" so government can catch up. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is investigating AI's "existential risk," while Sens. John Thune (R-S.D.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) are pursuing a narrower plan requiring companies to test and report catastrophic risks. Reality check: Political pressure and lobbying could crack open the door to narrow bipartisan measures, though any meaningful regulation would still have to survive Trump's veto pen. The bottom line: Washington is deeply divided on whether AI is a national triumph to unleash or a national emergency to contain.

d1af408bfaae.text:
At a moment when the US is reconsidering the extent and purpose of its engagement abroad, I find myself returning to a lesson I confronted often in my time in government: After more than five decades working on Africa, one of the most important things the US can do is show up and listen.
The story of how the African Growth and Opportunity Act came together in 1999 is instructive as I recall in my memoir. We were preparing to roll out AGOA under the Clinton administration and invited the leadership of the African diplomatic corps to the State Department for a briefing. We told the ambassadors that only 10 countries would be selected and that their governments would be informed through our ambassadors in Africa.
That went over like a lead balloon.
The dean of the group, the highly respected Roble Olhaye of Djibouti, reminded us that the diplomatic corps had been advocating for AGOA for five years. They had been updating their capitals and lobbying Congress for the legislation. How, he asked, could we treat them in such a âshabby manner?â
He was right. We had not been listening.
So we changed course, inviting more than 180 ministers from 43 African countries to Washington for four days of discussions with President Bill Clinton, cabinet members, Congress, business leaders, and civil society representatives to discuss trade, investment, conflict prevention, food security, democracy, and human rights.
We then went back to the list of potential AGOA beneficiaries and determined that 32 African countries met the conditions of the legislation.
The rest, as they say, is history.
More than a quarter-century later, AGOA is again in flux. Congress extended the program through the end of 2026, and the Trump administration has said it wants to modernize the legislation to align with its America First trade policy and create more opportunities for US businesses.
This creates an opportunity to ask a bigger question: What should the US-Africa commercial relationship look like for the next 25 years?
The answer should not be developed in Washington alone.
Africa has changed dramatically since AGOA was created. It is building a continent-wide market, while its governments are seeking investment in manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, and technology, while looking to add value to their mineral resources.
The US has interests of its own: new markets for American companies, resilient supply chains, and access to critical minerals. Those interests can align with African priorities, but Washington should not assume they do.
That is why listening is a strategic tool, not simply a diplomatic courtesy. If Washington wants American companies to compete more effectively in Africa, it first needs to understand what its potential partners actually want.
That is why the Trump administration should convene the US-Africa Ministerial called for in the recently extended AGOA legislation â and make the meeting more than a ceremonial gathering. It should bring together African governments, continent-wide blocs such as the African Union, US and African businesses, investors, and civil society to help shape the next generation of the relationship.
The goal should be more than modernizing a trade preference program. It should be to identify where US and African interests genuinely intersect â and where they do not â and build policy around that reality.
There is a broader lesson here for US policy toward Africa. A relationship centered more heavily on trade, investment, and mutually beneficial commercial opportunities can be entirely consistent with Americaâs interests.
But transactional does not have to mean transactional-only.
The most successful commercial relationships are built on knowledge, trust, and sustained engagement. My experience in 1999 taught me that showing up is not enough. You have to listen before you decide what the partnership should look like.
That is as true for the next 25 years as it was for the first 25.
Witney W. Schneidman is the author of This Africa Idea: A Memoir of Discovery, Diplomacy, and Opportunity, published by Bloomsbury. He served as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Africa during the Clinton Administration.

234f157945f1.text:
The News
Uber was paying Nigerian drivers more than it charged passengers for some short trips, an unsustainable subsidy that played a leading role in the US ride-hailing giantâs abrupt exit this month, according to a new report based on thousands of Uber trips.
The company quit Nigeria and Uganda on Sept. 2, the same day it announced a global restructuring decision that cut 10% of its staff globally. It still operates in four African countries including South Africa and Kenya.
Even after 12 years of operating in Nigeria, Uber did not have a large enough number of active passengers there and high inflation and currency depreciation made passengers increasingly price sensitive, according to a report by Obi, a California-based price and trip data aggregator that tracks more than half-dozen ride hailing platforms.
âItâs obvious that demand [in Nigeria] was low and that the political and economic climate wasnât helping,â Ashwini Anburajan, CEO of Obi, told Semafor. âPay had to be subsidized to make drivers willing to take rides. There was just no way for Uber to dig itself out of this pattern,â Anburajan said.
Her firmâs data suggests that Uber paid Nigerian drivers more than it charged passengers on trips shorter than 12 miles (20 km). In some cases, the company paid drivers 23% more than the passenger was actually charged. Though the company adjusted this pattern above the 12-mile threshold, it amounted to an âover-generousâ subsidy scheme for short rides that drivers would not have otherwise accepted, an approach that Uberâs in-country rivals like InDrive did not resort to, Obi said.
A typical Uber driver in Nigeria averaged 130 rides over the first seven months of 2026, but that was just over a tenth of the volume of rides the companyâs drivers in South Africa fulfilled over the same period, the report first shared with Semafor showed. Yet, Nigerian drivers kept a larger share of the fare paid by passengers compared to their counterparts in South Africa, the firm said. Its report is based on data from more than 20,000 rides completed by more than 300 drivers within the period on Uber and InDrive, a Russian-founded US company that also operates in Nigeria.
Step Back
Uberâs arrival in Nigeria in 2014 heralded a taxi revolution after a couple handful of startups attempted ride-hailing services in Lagos with little success. The company rode in aggressively with more than a billion dollars in investor capital to upstage the cityâs often rickety yellow cabs, promising technology-aided transport efficiency to passengers and dependable income to drivers.
This monthâs decision to pull out came after several attempts to stay relevant, from floating courier services and boat taxis, to multiple fare rises implemented to reflect higher costs of doing business following economic policy changes that have been rolled out since 2023.
Fuel prices have risen more than five-fold in Nigeria since the end of a government fuel subsidy scheme, and the naira currency has depreciated by more than 70% in that period, a combination that depresses net incomes both for drivers and transport companies. Some Nigeria analysts have cited a âchallenging macroeconomic environmentâ as the root cause of Uberâs exit as more expensive taxis became less preferred to relatively cheaper alternatives like buses, tricycles and motorcycles.
Know More
InDrive and Estonian company Bolt were Uberâs main Nigeria competitors and are now the main beneficiaries of the latterâs exit. Their ability to tweak parts of their operations to local sensibilities â like InDriveâs bargaining feature, and Boltâs flexibility with trip cancellation, car models and payment options â diminished the advantages Uber had gained from a two-year headstart, some analysts have argued.
Bolt, which pushed into offering three-wheeled taxis outside of Lagos, had won 60% of Nigeria market share by the time of Uberâs exit, Obi said. Active Nigerian users reached 3.3 million last December, more than six times that of Uber, according to Sensor Tower, a California-based app usage tracker.
Anburajan agrees with the view that localization may have helped Uber. âKeeping your business model and experience for users and drivers relatively uniform across markets can work if your target riders are international travelers who will place value on an experience thatâs the same from one country to the next,â she said. Ride-hailing will remain compelling and competitive in Africa for companies with âan approach that works for locals,â she said.
Ultimately, though, size does not equal a large opportunity. The upshot of Obiâs report is that there is simply no scale for Uber to absorb losses that must inevitably result from âa bad combinationâ of low per-driver volume and a per-ride subsidy. âA platform that has to raise prices by 71% and still needs to subsidize a large share of its rides is in a structural hole it canât price its way out of.â
Room for Disagreement
Some analysis of Uberâs exit blames the company for undercutting Nigerian drivers through unilateral fare cuts, prompting the drivers to revolt and port to rivals like Bolt.
On the other hand, the exit may be due to a shift in long-term priorities. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the 10% cut to the companyâs global staff was about âfocusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us.â That has been widely interpreted as reflecting Uberâs increasing shift towards self-driving taxis, evidenced by the companyâs rollout of 15 robotaxis in London after the headcount cut. It is a line of business that is not yet viable in most African cities due to under-developed road networks and other factors.
Notable
- Uberâs Nigeria exit and overall experience in Africa âundercuts the assumption that U.S. technology companies will inevitably dominate every market they enter,â Onyeka Aralu, a competition fellow at the International Center for Law & Economics in Oregon, argues.

a3cfcdb6206c.text: By — Alex Veiga, Associated Press Alex Veiga, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/what-to-know-about-recent-dire-ai-predictions-and-calls-for-safeguards Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about recent dire AI predictions and calls for safeguards Science Sep 14, 2026 8:09 AM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — New warnings from within the artificial intelligence industry have revived a long-running debate over whether advanced AI could escape human control and ultimately threaten humanity's survival, and whether the companies developing the technology are doing enough to prevent such a scenario. The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work, cautioning Saturday that a swarm of AI agents might be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless companies devoted more time to putting safeguards in place. READ MORE: Anthropic CEO says AI industry needs to give safety measures time to catch up Dario Amodei outlined a plan for companies like his and governments around the world to ensure that increasingly capable AI models remain aligned with the commands and values of responsible people days after two former Anthropic safety researchers publicly aired concerns that the existential threats AI might pose to humanity were receiving too little attention. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Here's what to know about the recent dire predictions and whether any brakes might be put on AI advancement. AI models are becoming more powerful Concerns over the potential risks of the technology are rising as new AI models become more powerful, heightening both the potential for misuse by people with criminal aims, such as creating and spreading a disease that kills most of the world's population, and the risk of AI systems going rogue in a dangerous way. Anthropic disclosed last week that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons. WATCH: AI researcher warns companies are ignoring catastrophic risks The company said it put stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could be used to make weapons but noted that "as models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society's defenders act to make them safer." Last year, Anthropic reported that hackers used the company's AI in a cyberattack targeting about 30 companies and government agencies around the world. It said the hackers were very likely from a Chinese state-sponsored group. Multiple AI models have acted on their own When an AI agent "goes rogue," it means the AI has taken action beyond the task it was asked to perform. Both Anthropic and OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, said in July that their AI models had succeeded in acting on their own. Anthropic disclosed that three AI models — Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model — hacked into three other organizations during testing just days after OpenAI revealed that its AI system hacked into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face. READ MORE: Senators from both parties question OpenAI on breach of AI startup Hugging Face OpenAI described the intrusion by a combination of models, including its newly released GPT‑5.6 Sol and an "even more capable" model that was still being tested internally, as a "significant security incident." Meta followed suit in early August with a similar case of an AI model finding ways around another company's digital security. Although some observers noted that people had disabled some guardrails in the OpenAI and Anthropic cases, the episodes seemed to reflect one of the biggest fears around AI: that if models achieve artificial general intelligence, or AGI, a loosely defined term for AI that can match or surpass human abilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks, the technology could cause an irreversible catastrophic event or subjugate the human race. How or when AI might cause a catastrophe is debated Doomsday scenarios generally fall into two categories: An AI that achieves self-improving superintelligence controls people instead of vice versa, or AI used by a rogue state or nefarious actors. Worries that artificial intelligence might overcome human limits on its reach or actions are not new. READ MORE: AI agents are hacking systems without any input from humans. How did we get here? Alan Turing, a British mathematician widely regarded as one of the earliest authorities on artificial intelligence, predicted in 1951 that AI would eventually take control from humans. Less than a decade later, Norbert Wiener, another mathematician, warned intelligent machines would seek to accomplish their own objectives and humans would not be able to stop them. In 2026, how reasonable are fears that AI, either by escaping human control or through misuse by unscrupulous people, could cause a cataclysmic event or the downfall of civilization? No one knows. Experts across computer science, philosophy and other fields have envisioned numerous routes by which a future AI system might cause a global catastrophe, either by escaping human control or in the hands of an unscrupulous people. They range from deploying weapons and identifying a lethal pathogen to manipulating governments into conflict or disrupting the food, energy and communications networks societies rely on to function. There is no widely accepted estimate for how soon any of these scenarios might happen and no consensus on their likelihood. Africaâs richest man Aliko Dangote tapped the opening gong this morning on the floor of the Lagos exchange to open Africaâs largest initial public offer.
The $20 billion Dangote Refinery built on swamp land on the outskirts of Lagos becomes the fourth Dangote Industries subsidiary to go public in Nigeria. When the initial offer closes next month, the company will have raised more than $4 billion at about a $50 billion valuation, if demand matches the year-long buzz partly driven by the companyâs pledge to pay dividends in US dollars. The refinery will likely account for up to 40% of the Lagos exchangeâs capitalization when its shares start trading post IPO in November.
âWe are going to fully, fully share all our prosperity with the people,â Dangote, 69, said in a packed and celebratory hall of bankers, investors and stock brokers for whom the multibillion-dollar Dangote Refinery IPO has been the most talked-about business event in Nigeria all year.
âWe, as a group, will list every single company that we operate,â he said, flanked on either side by two of his three adult daughters. Each of them holds an executive role in the Dangote conglomerate and they are positioned to lead its future, but it is the grey-haired veteran magnate who turns the newest page of the empireâs 45-year-old history.
The capital raise and market lead are steps to a more expansive ambition: Dangoteâs push to be the biggest fuel seller to Africaâs 1.5 billion people.
âWe want to displace less competitive imports that are coming from far away into a market that we can better serve in closer proximity,â David Bird, an ex-Shell executive who has been the Dangote Refineryâs CEO for a year, told Semafor in an interview. Rather than seeing Europe or elsewhere as an export market to target, the refineryâs goal is to win over all of those regionsâ fuel supply businesses in Africa, he said.
Central to its strategy of meeting Africaâs fuel demand is an ongoing $14 billion project to double the Nigerian refineryâs output to make it the worldâs largest by the first quarter of 2029, Bird said. âWe will have foundations and steel coming out of the ground by the end of the year,â Bird said of the Nigeria expansion. The Dangote groupâs separate $16 billion Kenya plant is at the planning stage.
Bruce Tanner, the Nigerian refineryâs chief financial officer, told Semafor that âpretty much allâ of the IPO proceeds will go towards funding the plans, with additional debt equity financing on the horizon. Executing the expansion would provide an impetus for a secondary listing on an international exchange, he said.
Know More
Fuel consumption in Nigeria has risen by about 7.5% on average annually since the Dangote Refinery began transporting fuel to Nigerian pump stations two-and-a-half years ago, despite higher fuel prices after President Bola Tinubu ended a government subsidy. Higher demand and global events, such as the disruption to oil supply sparked by the Iran war since February, have worked in the companyâs favor. It netted $1.8 billion in profit after tax on nearly $14 billion of revenue in the first half of this year, more than its total revenue for 2025.
FirstCap, a Nigerian investment bank that is one of two dozen co-issuers of the IPO, expects the refineryâs revenue at the end of this year to reach $28 billion, more than double last yearâs earnings. Nigeriaâs 220 million population makes it Africaâs largest fuel market. Its growing population and fast pace of urbanization will keep the demand trend for the refinery upwards, according to the bank and other equity analysts.
But serving other African markets â from Senegal to Namibia â that have historically depended on imports from Europe and the Middle East is the pillar of the Dangote refineryâs long-term growth, Bird said. A key part of the whole expansion push is to build out âstructural distribution infrastructureâ made up of regional tank farms and pipelines that will connect the groupâs refineries to prospective markets on the continent, he said. Executing these plans would be very rewarding for the company. Revenue is projected to grow at an average of 45% per year between this year and 2030, according to FirstCap, with a three-fold increase in pre-tax profit to $13 billion within the period.
With expansion years away, solving current operational challenges is critical to the refineryâs pitch that the IPO will be a wealth creation platform for everyday Nigerians. One of those challenges is ensuring regular access to crude oil.
Step Back
On more than one occasion this year, Bird has publicly raised alarm concerning unreliable crude oil supply from Nigeria, particularly under a government scheme aimed to insulate the refineryâs crude purchase price from foreign exchange volatility (the refinery temporarily switched to pricing fuel sales in dollars in July). The company still sources up to 35% of feedstock under that scheme, but a similar share has also come from abroad.
âWeâve got to get everyone off this idea that weâre wedded to Nigerian crude. Itâs not about Nigerian crude,â Bird said. The company has bought from several African countries, including Angola, Cameroon, Ghana, and Senegal. It bought two cargoes from the UAE in June, its first crude purchase from the Middle East. With the prospect of an expanded refining capacity in the near future, Bird plans to be even less reliant on Nigerian supply as the business expands and pursues exports to regional markets.
âOur sole business model is daily margin maximization. Iâm completely agnostic to where the crude comes from,â he said.
Room for Disagreement
Feyi Fawehinmi, a UK-based accountant and author, and a long-time Dangote critic, said investors in the IPO âare being asked to pay a lot more for each dollar of Dangote Refineryâs earnings,â based on his comparison of the plantâs finances against those of four peer refiners in India, South Korea, Turkey, and the US.Fawehinmi argues that the IPO is the latest evide

"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," Furlong said in the post. Pennsylvania's two previous measles-related deaths involved infants. Both occurred in August and a coroner reported that the virus itself caused one of the deaths. The first dose of measles vaccine is typically given to infants around 1 year old, meaning neither infant was old enough to be vaccinated. READ MORE: There are already more U.S. measles cases this year than in all of 2025 As of Friday, Pennsylvania had 676 measles cases in 37 of the state's 67 counties. Of those cases, 124 involved hospitalizations and four people who were vaccinated against measles, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. The three measles-related deaths reported by state and local officials as of Sunday did not square with figures of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which showed no such deaths this year. "The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause," read the CDC website Sunday. Pennsylvania's Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and Republican President Donald Trump's administration have clashed over details of the two previous deaths in the state.
