Keating, the top Democrat on the committeeâs Europe panel, was joined by every other panel Democrat as well as the top Democrat on the full committee. The panel will hold a hearing Tuesday morning on the Balkans.
Know More
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have called on the Trump administration to impose sanctions on Dodik and other Serbian officials in Bosnia amid concerns that their recent actions could destabilize the region. Republika Srpska, the Serbian enclave, has devoted at least $9 million to winning over the Trump administration since the presidentâs second inauguration.
Tuesdayâs report raises questions about Joseph Flynn and Jesse Binnallâs campaign to build the Bosnian Southern Interconnection Gas Pipeline, worth some $1.16 billion, âdespite no prior energy sector or regional experience.â The pair sought to profit from Bosniaâs energy sector âat the expense of the Bosnian people,â the report argues, including by establishing AAFS Infrastructure & Energy four days after US and Bosnian officials discussed the possibility of a US firm building the pipeline.
âI am troubled that the potential awarding of this contract to an inexperienced firm decreases the likelihood the pipeline will be put into operation,â Keating wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in April. âAdditionally, the personal and political ties between AAFS and the Trump administration represent an unfair conflict of interest.â
A State Department official argued in response that âthe decisions to offer a concession for the Southern Interconnection and to select a US company as the lead investor were the
sovereign choices made by Federation of BiH officials.â That âcontradicts the Trump administrationâs policy decisions, which advocated for AAFS to be the sole concessionaire for the project,â according to the report.
âOur involvement began when Bosnian government officials approached AAFS directly about participating,â Binnall told Semafor, calling the pipeline âa critically important piece of infrastructure for Americaâs and regionâs energy future.â
âWe then engaged with career officials at the US Embassy, the standard, expected practice for any US-based company operating abroad on a project of this scale,â he added.
Adrian Elimian contributed to this report.

d6073ccccbdb.text:
Ashleyâs view
AI companies are stirring up a maelstrom right now by essentially reminding Washington of whatâs been true for years: Theyâre not outright opposed to regulation.
Some support certain safety proposals at the federal, state, and even international levels. This dates back to the dawn of consumer-facing chatbot AI, which didnât have a long honeymoon period as exciting and life-changing tech. Americans were too jaded from the mid-2010s backlash to social media, and its subsequent lack of government regulation.
So what are we really seeing play out this week? As the voting public starts internalizing the risks of AI on a new level, the industry is evolving how it applies the big lessons it learned from the techlash. Call it recursive self-improvement, the lobbying version.
It starts with the core conclusion that AI companies have drawn from their social media counterparts: Shaping regulation to your liking is better than trying to convince everyone youâre harmless. Since ChatGPT rolled out nearly four years ago, even the loudest AI enthusiasts have stressed a need to balance âthe promise and the perilâ of the technology.
When OpenAI and Anthropic set up shop in DC, they hired former high-ranking Democratic and Republican officials; people who had been in the policy trenches during the first round of high-profile Capitol Hill hearings featuring tech executives; and savvy partisan kingmakers.
Theyâve been on defense since they first established offices in Washington, and right now theyâre playing the most sophisticated version around. That has involved proposing multiple paths for action, as OpenAI and Anthropic have done â encouraging certain congressional efforts, endorsing some state lawmaking, and offering coordinated self-regulation in the meantime.
Which brings up another lesson AI companies have learned: They can live with a series of similar state-level regulations, which are often a safer bet than banking on Washington to establish national standards.
Fanning out to statehouses for AI lobbying is often an easier lift than getting Congress to do much of anything. OpenAIâs top political strategist, Chris Lehane, calls it âreverse federalism.â
Know More
AI faces the same divides that have plagued every previous tech policy debate, and it is more complicated and fast-moving than any of its tech predecessors. Unresolved issues run the gamut, from antitrust protections to chip export controls to whether existing consumer laws are sufficient to protect people from harmful AI.
Thatâs not to mention privacy and cybersecurity, which government agencies should be involved, and who defines âsafeâ AI.
Where there is consensus about what to do, there is a lack of political power. Where the power concentrates, in the White House, there is no desire to lay down stricter rules.
âThere is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and data centers,â President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social Monday, later calling anti-AI sentiment a âhoax.â
Vice President JD Vance, seemingly more cognizant that public sentiment is shifting away from AI, said that âwe want to make sure we regulate smartly and weâre thoughtful about the risk.â
Then he acknowledged the gamesmanship playing out: âI feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them; it feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse.â
Itâs more like an industry whose messaging is, for now, staying ahead of the storm. AI companies donât have to agree on a legislative approach when Congress canât agree. All they have to do is sound open â and prepare for a classic DC regulatory quagmire.
Room for Disagreement
A challenging path to legislation wonât stop AI from dominating the political landscape. AI safety advocates, Democrats, and some Republicans will keep pushing on the issue to draw helpful contrasts in the midterm elections.
The strange coalition of populists and progressives who want to curb AI will gather in Washington today for a âPro-Human Assembly.â Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., and former White House adviser Steve Bannon will speak at what may be this weekâs only venue for bipartisan agreement on AI.
A flicker of hope for action remains in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that his proposed AI safety bill, shaped with Texas Republican Ted Cruz and Minnesota Democrat Amy Klobuchar, would be introduced âhopefully soon.â
âI think there is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead,â Thune said.
The bill is unlikely to meet the mark for many Democrats, who fear it wonât go far enough.
Notable
- Trump met with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on the sidelines of last weekâs GOP midterm convention, MS NOW reports.
- Democratic contenders for the 2028 presidential race see an opportunity to define themselves on AI. See: Pete Buttigieg and Jon Ossoff.
Burgess Everett contributed to this report.

The News
The Trump administration is going all out to convince Senate Republicans to advance landmark cryptocurrency legislation over banksâ concerns.
Officials plan to launch an interactive tool on Tuesday that allows users âto set the parameters, run the scenarios, and see for themselvesâ why the Council of Economic Advisers previously concluded âthere is no meaningful relationship between stablecoin growth and community bank deposit flight,â Chair Chris Phelan told Semafor.
The goal: push back on banking groups, which said Monday that recent changes didnât go far enough to make them comfortable with the billâs stablecoin provisions.
Multiple Republican lawmakers, including Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, have indicated they could take the banksâ side by voting ânoâ on Tuesday afternoon.
Crypto-friendly Democrats, meanwhile, are unhappy with the extent to which the latest text would rein in President Donald Trump.
Know More
âIâm not sure [the latest text] addresses the issues Iâm concerned about, which is what community bankers are concerned about,â Cornyn told Semafor Monday night. He added that heâs âlooking forward to having a conversation and seeing where the votes are.â
The bill, which would divide oversight of digital assets between the SEC and CFTC, needs the support of at least 60 senators to move forward. CEAâs new website will also include an FAQ on its earlier report and responses to its critics.
âThe CEA analysis is clear: the data simply does not support the deposit flight narrative that DC bank lobbyists are pushing on stablecoin rewards,â Patrick Witt, executive director of the presidentâs Council of Advisers for Digital Assets, said. He added that the Clarity Act âincludes real safeguards to protect community banks if the deposit flight scenario ever did materializeâ but âbanks get none of those protections if the bill fails.â
Crypto-friendly Democrats have focused their criticism on revised ethics provisions that they say still donât do enough to curtail Trump. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., argued they would âcover federal employees other than the president, functionallyâ and ânot apply, in the current form, to the first family.â
âI donât think the ethics provision is near enough,â Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said. âIâm really concerned.â
But theyâre keeping their powder mostly dry as they seek to respond to the latest draft before Tuesdayâs vote. Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said he had several issues with the bill but would âcontinue to engage and pushâ on the ethics provisions âbecause right now, we donât have any real rulesâ for digital assets.
âA week ago I would have said that didnât look good, but weâll see if thatâs changed,â Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor.
Step Back
The crypto industry is waiting on the vote to deploy tens of millions of dollars in campaign cash. That war chest doesnât loom as large as it did last cycle, given how little time remains before midterms, how few Senate Democrats are up for reelection in competitive races â and, most crucially, how many progressives are seizing on it as a political liability.
âNo one whoâs in-cycle caresâ about the money, a Senate Democratic aide said. Compared to spring 2024, âitâs just not that much of a concern anymore.â
Thatâs not true for everyone: Some House Democrats were panicked Monday that the industryâs leading network of super PACs may not spend in their races despite their support of the bill earlier this Congress, people familiar with their thinking told Semafor. Some of the legislationâs top House Democratic backers hail from purple districts where they would benefit from any outside help.
âWhen it comes to a statewide general election, the vast majority of voters are just seeing the ads that are playing between now and November, not double-clicking to see or care who is funding them,â a cryptocurrency executive said.
A person close to crypto PAC Fairshake told Semafor that its plans for this cycle havenât been finalized or shared. The person added that Fairshake has already spent more than $30 million on Democratic candidates this cycle.
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., is still undecided, he told Semafor Monday night. The Georgia Democrat is his caucusâ only incumbent in a tough race.
âI havenât read it yet,â Ossoff said. âI read things before I vote.â

7ae2acb15f6b.text:
IRONWOOD FOREST NATIONAL MONUMENT, Ariz.—Cassandra Becerra didn’t know it when she first arrived in the U.S. from Mexico as a three-year-old, but she was already an environmentalist. Her family didn’t have much money, but they were rich in the abundant public lands that make up Arizona
Becerra remembers a childhood filled with fishing at the lake, playing with worms and exploring the desert. Those memories helped lead her down the path of working in the environmental space, serving as the Arizona State Director for Mountain Mamas, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting the environment for the next generation. On Saturday, they led her to stand before a mountain range in the Ironwood Forest National Monument just north of Tucson to kick off the 12th annual Latino Conservation Week, a nationwide initiative created by the Hispanic Access Foundation to inspire the Latino community to connect with the outdoors and advocate for the protection of the country’s natural resources.
“We’ve been caring for these places that we’ve called home for so long, and not only that, but sharing our knowledge across generations and keeping our culture alive, spending time outdoors and protecting our resources,” Becerra said at the press conference opening the event. “We were taught these things by our families growing up and so that helped shape us. Latino Conservation Week really just encourages us to participate at a greater capacity to protect our environment and our natural resources.”
Kickstarting the week at Ironwood Forest National Monument was a strategic choice. Since it was designated as a monument in 2000, this stretch of 129,000 acres of the Sonoran Desert north of Tucson, Arizona, has been protected as a haven for scientific research and a buffer against the expansion of existing mines and the establishment of new ones in the area. It is also one of six national monuments the Trump administration has signaled it may reduce in size to make way for more development and extraction. Just outside of the monument is ASARCO’s Silver Bell mine, whose years-long goal of expanding into the area to boost copper production has been foiled by the site’s protections.
Locals fear another attempt to reduce the monument’s size may come soon. In July, President Donald Trump signed two executive orders drastically reducing the size of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments in southern Utah, a decision that has drawn sharp criticism from locals and led to lawsuits.
“Public lands belong to all of us, not special interests. Yet this summer, the Trump administration virtually eliminated Utah’s Grand Staircase Escalante and Bears Ears National Monuments, making them vulnerable to mining and drilling,” said Rebecca Perez, the Arizona conservation manager for the Wilderness Society, at the press conference. “Once these places are industrialized, they cannot be readily restored … Any effort to undo protections at one national monument is a threat to every national monument, including the one we stand at today.”
The week’s events across Arizona and the country to get Latino community members outdoors and involved with their public lands include hikes, cleanups and educational sessions. The first step to getting people involved in protecting the country’s natural spaces is to get them out in nature, the organizers said.
Before leading a small hike to explore the monument’s plant life, Christine Flanagan, president of the Friends of Ironwood Forest, recalled a walk in the desert with her grandmother when she was about six years old. Gesturing to the hills on the horizon, Flanagan’s grandmother told her never to let anyone tell her she wasn’t allowed there. These are public lands, she learned, and the public owns them.
“We all must join together and understand that this is our land,” Flanagan said. “And as public land owners, we need to start acting together like we own this land.”
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.
Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.
Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?
Please take a moment to make a tax-deductible donation. Every one of them makes a difference.
Thank you,

Second time’s the charm?
On Aug. 25, Maine’s Public Utilities Commission selected winning proposals in a years-long effort to turn more of northern Maine’s howling winds into energy that can power population centers in the southern part of the state and region.
The PUC selected one developer to build 800 megawatts of new onshore wind energy in Aroostook County—enough to power over 300,000 homes—and another to build a new transmission line capable of carrying up to 1,200 MW of power to Southern Maine and New England. Six hundred MW of the first tranche of power are reserved for Maine.
Advocates of renewable energy cheered the move.
“Maine has just said yes to 600 megawatts of clean energy—clean energy that is [at] a stable price, that is going to increase reliability and that is going to bring a whole host of economic benefits to Maine people,” said Eliza Donoghue, executive director of the Maine Renewable Energy Association.
Unlike the first time it ran this procurement, Maine did so in collaboration with four other New England states—Vermont, Rhode Island, Connecticut and Massachusetts—whose residents will help pay for the transmission line via charges on their utility bills, even as two of those states elected not to sign long-term deals for the new power.
Many steps remain before construction on the projects can commence, including securing all necessary local, state and federal approvals. If all goes to plan, power will flow across the new line in the “early 2030s,” according to PUC Chair Phil Bartlett.
That power is projected to boost grid reliability and cut both planet-warming emissions and costs, especially during the winter months when gas-fired power plants—the single largest source of electricity in New England—are more expensive to run, while wind speeds tend to be at their highest.
The scant public information about the project, however, left some critical of the process. “We don’t actually have enough information on the RFP portion to be able to make any kind of determination whether it’s great or not,” said Tanya Blanchard, co-founder and board president of Preserve Rural Maine, an organization that formed in response and opposition to the transmission line proposed last time this project was bid.
Among the remaining unknown details are the price for the power, the exact route the proposed transmission line will take, and the breakdown of how much each state’s ratepayers will pay for the transmission line.
Bartlett said that many of these details would be made public once contracts are finalized and defended the commission’s practice of secrecy before then. “There’s always the chance that things don’t get finalized and you’re going back out and you wouldn’t want to provide sort of unfair information to other competitors,” Bartlett said.
Federal approvals remain dicey under the presidential administration of Donald Trump, which has used every tool at its disposal to block the development of domestic wind power, even while power costs and demand have soared.
Perils Ahead
The first required federal approval will come not from a department of the Trump administration but from the independent Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).
FERC will need to approve the contract that the five states are still finalizing with the project developer, Avangrid.
Federal law typically limits FERC’s review of such contracts to about 60 days.
If FERC approves the transmission contract, Avangrid will still need state permits from the Maine PUC and Department of Environmental Protection. It would likely need U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approval as well, if the route crosses waterways or wetlands. At some point in those processes, the proposed transmission route would become public.
Environmental organizations cheered the progress toward new wind power while stopping short of supporting the wind and transmission projects until their environmental impacts are identified.
“With careful siting, thoughtful design, and responsible operation, the clean energy projects identified today will deliver reliable, affordable electricity to Mainers while reducing the pollution that is threatening our health and fueling changes to our climate that are already being felt across the state,” read a joint statement from the Natural Resources Council of Maine, Maine Audubon, Maine Conservation Alliance, Conservation Law Foundation and Acadia Center.
Avangrid is the parent company of Central Maine Power, the utility that delivers electricity to most Maine customers and has been locked in a months-long struggle with the PUC over its petition to further raise rates at a time of widely perceived energy unaffordability.
The PUC has said that this project will offer some relief, claiming it will net ratepayer benefits of $387 million to $425 million over its lifetime, factoring in all transmission costs. That number does not include local economic benefits or the benefits of avoided greenhouse gas emissions, but could not be independently verified.
To provide those cost savings, however, the turbines need to get built. San Francisco-based Clearway Energy Group will be responsible for building the wind farm.
Clearway’s senior director of communications, Zadie Oleksiw, told Inside Climate News that the company would proceed with seeking its own permit approvals “concurrently” with the transmission permitting.
Bartlett said the power purchase agreement that Maine is still finalizing with Clearway will be “contingent on” the transmission line receiving necessary approvals. In other words, construction on the generation project would likely not begin before all transmission approvals are finalized.

Iran strikes exposed gaps in medical evacuation ops across Middle East: IG
Medical professionals have long warned that drones would cause higher U.S. battlefield casualties. A new Inspector General report shows the military is still scrambling to meet that challenge.
The military abandoned plans to use Army helicopters to evacuate wounded troops involved in the war with Iran, and instead resorted to slower ground-based evacuations, in part due to the threat of drone strikes, according to a Defense Department Office of the Inspector General report released Monday. The shift illustrates a problem medical officials had warned about for years.
At the start of the operation, the U.S. used Army helicopters in Kuwait and Iraq for medical evacuation, but then moved them due to concerns about Iranian drone and missile strikes.
“Most evacuations during [Operation Epic Fury] were ultimately conducted by ground,” according to the report. In addition to the drone threat, the United States had the additional hurdle of relying on host country hospitals for what’s called “advanced, hospital level care” for particularly severe injuries, since establishing such hospitals on U.S. bases would require a large and more targetable footprint.
The move follows warnings from medical officials that future conflicts would be more dangerous for U.S. troops, as adversaries develop more advanced weapons—particularly drones. A 2022 Army University Press article by Lt. Col. Matthew Marsh and Capt. Ryan Hampton eerily forecasts the situation described in the inspector general report: “Medical personnel will experience intermittent air and ground evacuation with medical logistics constraints,” it reads.
Just as new technology has allowed some adversaries to become more dangerous and inflict higher casualties, other pressures led to cutbacks in medical evacuation capability, particularly in the Middle East. A July 2025 Pulse of Army Medicine article by Sgt. Maj. Sandra Johnson describes how, across U.S. Central Command, “Due to competing requirements, many of these bases only have one medic on post and no medical provider. A medic may have to care for a patient for several hours until they arrive at a local national hospital.”
She noted specifically the problem of “no Medical Evacuation (MEDEVAC) by flight or ground capability, or only ground Casualty Evacuation (CASEVAC) options,” across CENTCOM.
An April U.S. Naval Institute report explains: “Drone warfare [in Ukraine] has disrupted casualty movement from the point of injury throughout the combat casualty continuum of care.”
The IG report acknowledges that CENTCOM officials worked to rapidly develop new plans and strategies when faced with Iranian drone capabilities, moving troops and materiel.. “During OEF, USCENTCOM shifted personnel, assets, and storage facilities as locations came under Iranian and proxy attacks,” it reads.
The report carries a strong recommendation: To find and fix “the gaps in [Department of Defense counter-drone] interoperability, and the corrective actions needed to standardize” those capabilities.

- Published
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.
The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".
Moscow has not commented on the incident.
It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."
Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.
The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.
President Gitanas NausÄda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.
Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".
Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

ddaca86b317c.text:
Andyâs view
The late Henry Kissinger initially made his name as an academic writing about nuclear arms control during the Cold War, and latterly forged his reputation as the architect of US-China detente.
In his final years, however, Kissinger was fixated on what he believed to be an even greater danger: For the first time in human history, he observed, a technology â self-learning machines â could potentially target anything, anywhere, with any kind of destruction, making the world â100% vulnerable.â
He had become an AI doomer. And he pleaded for the US and China to open talks to avoid âcatastrophic consequences.â The template would be nuclear arms control agreements with the Soviet Union, which he himself negotiated.
Alas, Kissinger may have been uncannily prescient about technology and its impact on global power, but his prescriptions on how to avert AI disaster havenât aged well. As US President Donald Trump prepares for a summit this month with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Cold War analogies have become pointless â and the reasons why are instructive.
Beijing refuses to consider nuclear arms-limitation talks for precisely the reasons it would balk at joining the US in slowing AI progress, or âpacing the frontierâ in tech jargon.
The US has many more nuclear warheads. It also has at least a six-month lead in AI models, and vastly more compute. From Beijingâs perspective, restraint in both domains would only lock in Washingtonâs advantages, leaving China open to bullying and blackmail. No Chinese leader would perform that kind of kowtow.
For similar reasons, China spurns guardrails. Moscow and Washington had elaborate protocols to avoid inadvertent escalation during the Cold War, but Beijing thinks they would simply encourage US recklessness: The US and China canât even agree on ârules-of-the-roadâ to prevent accidents involving ships and planes in geopolitical flashpoints, like the South China Sea, from spiraling into armed conflict.
Some analysts argue that the Obama administration set a hopeful precedent on AI cooperation by coaxing China to join the Paris Climate Agreement in 2016. But that, too, is a stretch. In fact, China had its own powerful reasons to sign up for climate action, not least a public revolt against killer smog blanketing its megacities, and a security imperative to swap out imported oil for home-grown green technologies.
On the present trajectory, the US and China are hurtling toward the very calamity that Kissinger warned about.
US President Donald Trump is no Nixon. In the run-up to next weekâs meeting, heâs framed the stakes in zero-sum terms. âWeâre leading China in AI,â he told reporters over the weekend. âAnd frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.â
Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary whoâs preparing the summit, put it even more starkly, warning that if the US loses the AI race to China, âthere is no day after tomorrow.â
This is classic game theory that calls to mind the chilling 1950s debates over second strikes and counterforce. Both sides have a clear interest in slowing the development of the most advanced AI models â the Hugging Face attack was a wake-up call in the US; China has been confronted with the prospect of rogue agents taking over WeChat, its ubiquitous chat and payments platform. But they donât trust each other enough to do so. Silicon Valley labs assume that if they pause, China will race ahead anyway.
In an interview with The Economist in 2023, just before his 100th birthday, Kissinger warned that the US and China had five to 10 years to avoid an AI disaster. The clock is ticking. But, for now at least, neither side is watching the dials.

be7129a6dc7b.text: The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is investigating a Russian oligarch's reported financial involvement in a celebration related to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding , Axios has learned. Why it matters: Garcia is poised to be Congress' lead investigator if Democrats retake the House. This probe offers a pretty good hint of the direction he'll go in that role. "Oversight Democrats are investigating the numerous ways in which the Trump family have sought to enrich themselves on the basis of their proximity to President Donald Trump," Garcia stated in a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. In a separate letter to Trump Jr. , Garcia wrote that ProPublica's reporting on Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev's role in funding the event "may be the most serious allegation against you to date." Driving the news: Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, provided hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of expenses for the May party in the Bahamas, according to ProPublica. Kremlev is close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his boxing organization is financed by Russian state-owned energy company Gazprom. The oligarch paid for one of the two private islands where the event was held and a fireworks show, according to ProPublica, despite Trump Jr.'s estimated $300 million net worth . A Trump Jr. spokesperson did not dispute the payments to ProPublica, telling the outlet Kremlev is "a personal friend of Don," but "not someone he has a business relationship with." Kremlev's press office told ProPublica the two met "a couple of years ago" and "have a friendly relationship," and that he has "never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances." Trump Jr.'s wife, Bettina Anderson, said in a statement on Instagram that it is "unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister," adding, "Friendship doesn't require a political motive." President Trump said in a statement to Axios shared by the White House press office that he has "no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn't pay for Don and Bettina's wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding." "It was an 'afterparty' given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party," he added. A representative for Trump Jr. did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Kremlev. The latest: In his letter to Wiles, Garcia wrote that he wants all "documents, records, and communications between the White House and Mr. Donald Trump, Jr., concerning Mr. Umar Kremlev," including any warnings about his ties to Putin. He asked whether Trump Jr. has a security clearance, whether he disclosed his ties to Kremlev to the White House, and if President Trump's absence from the ceremony was related to the oligarch's involvement. "Any possible foreign entanglement deserves close scrutiny," Garcia wrote, citing reports that Trump Jr. is a key political adviser to his father. Garcia requested Trump Jr. turn over an array of documents, including a full guest list, dates of contact between him and Kremlev, and any communications he has had with the White House or intelligence officials about Kremlev. He also wants records of "all purchases made for your wedding by foreign nationals and others on your behalf," and gifts he received from foreign nationals or "those with close ties to adversaries of the United States." He asked Trump Jr. if Mr. Kremlev has ever provided him "anything of value in exchange for favorable treatment by the U.S. government or information about the Trump Administration." Between the lines: As the top minority party member on the panel, Garcia is currently stuck making voluntary requests for information, which can easily be shrugged off by the administration and Trump family members. That all changes if Democrats win the House and he obtains the Oversight Committee gavel next January: He would be able to compel potential witnesses to testify and turn over documents.

5011ce21f4a8.text: House Democratic leadership is vocally opposing a Russia sanctions bill set to come to a vote this week, but not all of their members are comfortable taking that stance just yet. Why it matters: Republicans will reportedly need some Democratic votes to make up for defections from their isolationist wing and pass the measure. At issue for many Democrats is that the bill, named in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would allow the Trump administration to impose up to 100% tariffs on the five top importers of Russian oil. That has forced Democrats to choose between two issues that have become shibboleths for their party: support for Ukraine and opposition to giving President Trump more power to set trade policy. State of play: Reps. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Richard Neal (D-Mass.) — the ranking members of the House Foreign Affairs, Joint Economic and Ways & Means committees, respectively — announced their opposition to the bill in a joint statement last week. "House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good," they said. "This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable." Yes, but: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), an arch-centrist who often breaks with party leadership, told Axios last week he is "almost certainly going to be a 'yes' on the bill. "I think the sanctions [are good] but I am also generally supportive of tariffs," said Golden. The Maine Democrat has been his party's lone cheerleader for many of Trump's more controversial protectionist trade measures. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) , the co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus, told Axios she is "reviewing [the bill] very carefully" and "working with our Ukraine Caucus." "I think it's important to send Russia a message that she needs to stand down," Kaptur added. Rep. Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), the other Democratic co-chair of the Ukraine Caucus, told Axios last week he is going to "see what it looks like" and that his vote "depends on exact wording." Between the lines: Meeks and former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), another staunch Ukraine supporter, tried to get amendments to the bill to make the trade language more palatable. The Republican-controlled House Rules Committee rejected those proposed changes Monday and advanced the bill to a procedural vote on the House floor. The bill passed in an overwhelmingly bipartisan 86-11 Senate vote last month and is supported by the White House, but its momentum has slowed in the House.

Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara.
Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to". Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."
Noah Kahan then performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to actor and director Rob Reiner.
Heroes and Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, who died last month, was also remembered alongside other stars including Rocky Horror Show's Tim Curry and Dawson's Creek actor James Van Der Beek.
Emmy winner O'Hara, who died in January this year aged 71, was known for playing Culkin's frantic mother in the 1990s film franchise, as well as the eccentric Moira Rose - mum to Murphy and Levy's Alexis and Dan - in Schitt's Creek.
"You remember her as the forgetful mother, right?" said Culkin.
"There are all kinds of words I could use to describe Catherine. She was encouraging. She was warm. She was funny, but the word that I think of is mom... She was, she was my mom. She was our mom.
"So she may have forgotten me twice. But we will always remember her."
Murphy noted how, since her death, many people had quoted O'Hara's most memorable lines from her show back at her.
"These are only very few of the interactions I've been lucky enough to have that remind me how profoundly Catherine has impacted the world, and it's because she brought us joy," Murphy said.
Levy added: "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness."
The emotional moment, which featured a big image of a smiling O'Hara as the backdrop, appeared to bring actors Martin Short and Steve Martin, sitting in the audience, to tears.
Charlie's Angels remember
Reiner, who died last December, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.
Reiner was killed along with his wife last year.
A tearful Jamie Lee Curtis paid tribute to the director, writer and performer, who made films such as When Harry Met Sally, This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, Misery and A Few Good Men, calling him a "cherished legend" and "our beloved meathead".
The 48-year gap between Reiner's two most recent Emmy wins set a new record, beating his Dad, Carl Reiner.
Curtis began her speech by first acknowledging the passing of Cheers co-creator James Burrows, who was also a good friend of Reiner's.
There were also warm words for Farrah Fawcett, who died in 2009.
Celebrating 50 years, Charlie's Angels stars Kate Jackson, Cheryl Ladd and Jaclyn Smith, handed out the Emmy for best drama and paid tribute to their fellow Angel.
Jackson said Fawcett "was the shiniest angel of all, and she was loved by millions of people all over the world. And she still is today. And they'll never forget her and neither will we. And I'm sure you won't either."
Buffy the Vampire Slayer stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreana paid tribute to the co-stars they have lost recently, including Nicholas Brendon, Anthony Head and Michelle Trachtenberg.
Geller said: "David and I would like to acknowledge that it has been a tough two years for our beloved cast and crew, and we feel very lucky to have known and worked with such amazing people."
'God bless you Dolly'
Elsewhere on the night, Remarkably Smart Creatures actress Sally Field, who starred in Steel Magnolias opposite Dolly Parton, led a tribute to the country music star, who died last month.
Field described Parton as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny" as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire.
"She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy herself in 2021.
"God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on earth who will love you for ever and ever."

Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman says.
Oman's Maritime Security Centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room, adding that the vessel was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula.
On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route.
But the US military insisted the Iranian report was false. It said the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel that was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday.
Earlier this month, Iran made a similar claim about an incident that killed two Filipino sailors on a Saudi-owned oil supertanker in the crucial waterway.
The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel, Sidr, caught fire after hitting a naval mine. But Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran and maritime security firms reported that it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam.
The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

7bcf60ea967c.text:
Bogland
Merritt R. Turetsky
W.W. Norton & Company, $29.99
Thank goodness Merritt Turetsky became captivated by boglands. The ecosystem ecologist evocatively describes the beauty, danger and vitality of these ecosystems in her book, Bogland.
“Buffering the space between forest and river, boglands refuse to be defined as either land or water,” writes Turetsky, of the University of Colorado Boulder. Their soggy, oxygen-starved conditions make it difficult for microbes to break down organic matter, allowing carbon-rich peat to form. It’s that peat that sets boglands apart from all other ecosystems, she writes.
Boglands primarily consist of bogs and fens (and sometimes marshes and swamps). Bogs derive their water from precipitation, are lacking in nutrients and are known for sphagnum moss and carnivorous plants such as sundew and pitcher plants. Fens, in contrast, get their water from streams and groundwater as well as rain. Because fens have access to more nutrients, they support more diverse plant communities.
Anytime Turetsky dove into her own adventures in boglands, I was transfixed. It’s in these moments — trying to stay calm amid insect swarms, reaching her arms deep into the murk and wading through muck with other devoted scientists — that the book shines.
Turetsky’s bug baptism occurred on a college trip to a Nova Scotia bog as hundreds of mosquitoes, black flies and other insects quickly descended around her netted head. The sounds “are seared deep into my memory,” she writes. “After a half an hour I knew I needed to conquer the noise or be driven insane.”
In Brunei, Turetsky meets up with a peatland restoration research team. The group enters the waist-deep water, moves through a rehabilitated area, then reaches a healthy peat swamp. This secret garden, Turetsky writes, “is pure pitcher plant heaven — unlike anything in my northern bogs, with layers of pitcher plants not only growing on the ground but dangling from the trees.” The colors and shapes she describes reminded me of something Dr. Suess would dream up.
But along with their beauty and wonder, boglands harbor potential danger. Turetsky recalls getting lost when she ventured out alone to check something in a study plot. “Even in familiar terrain, boglands are deceiving,” she writes. “I was disoriented even as I felt surrounded by what seemed well-known.” Luckily, it wasn’t too long before she found her team — otherwise, they would have had to commence a search-and-rescue mission.
Turetsky’s devotion to boglands celebrates the contradictions in these ecosystems: Filled with decay but teeming with life; places of refuge and risk; an ally in a changing climate as well as a potential foe.
Peatlands occupy just 3 percent of the world’s land area but store around 30 percent of Earth’s soil carbon, Turetsky writes. “This far exceeds the carbon stored in the world’s forest biomass, despite forests covering a much larger area.”
However, boglands are being drained for agriculture and damaged by wildfires, drought and changing climate conditions. As more are destroyed, there is a serious threat that they could release their carbon stores, adding to greenhouse gas emissions, Turetsky notes.
I have a general understanding of climate science, but I wish Turetsky would have provided more basic information on that topic. Just as she lost her way in the bog, I got turned around by mentions of different warming periods and ice ages. But the bigger message of how boglands formed over geologic time and their contribution to Earth’s climate system still comes through.
Overall, my time spent in Bogland felt expertly navigated by Turetsky. I emerged firmly on team boglands. For me, the book’s ultimate gift was igniting a reverence for these incredible ecosystems. And to my great delight, Turetsky closes with a list of bogs, some with boardwalks, that people can visit. I’m grabbing my bug spray now.
Buy Bogland from Bookshop.org. Science News is a Bookshop.org affiliate and will earn a commission on purchases made from links in this article.

ef1fb9e871fc.text:
- Published
Prosecutors in Colombia have accused former foreign minister Laura Sarabia of abusing her power after she made her nanny take a lie detector test.
The scandal erupted in 2023, when Colombian news weekly Semana reported that a woman Sarabia had employed to look after her son had been hooked up to a polygraph and questioned over the alleged disappearance of a case full of cash from Sarabia's flat.
Sarabia, who was the chief of staff for President Gustavo Petro at the time, resigned in June 2023 but was later appointed as foreign minister and, following her resignation from that post, as Colombia's ambassador to the United Kingdom.
She has denied any wrongdoing.
The 32-year-old was one of the closest advisers of Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first left-wing president, who governed from 2022 to August this year.
Prosecutors said Sarabia abused her position as his chief of staff by ordering police to question her nanny, Marelbys Meza, over the alleged disappearance of the cash, which was said to amount to several thousands of dollars.
Meza told Semana that she was taken by Sarabia's driver to an official building opposite the presidential palace, saying it felt like "a kidnapping".
Police officers then attached her to a polygraph machine and questioned her about the alleged disappearance of the money.
Meza denied having stolen any money during the test, and has consistently denied any wrongdoing in media interviews since.
Prosecutors allege that in ordering police to question Meza, Sarabia improperly used state resources to investigate a matter which was not related to her official post.
Sarabia rejected the accusation during a hearing, without going into further details.
She had earlier said in a social media post that her lawyers were dealing with the issue and that she respected the judicial authorities and trusted their decisions.

eaa87cd3584c.text: The U.S. military destroyed two Iranian small boats Monday after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps tried to steal a Navy drone patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The unusual incident shows how efforts to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues direct confrontation with Iran . The U.S. military initially didn't disclose the strike, and Iranian media presented it as a drone strike on "fishing boats." Driving the news: According to Iranian media , two fishing boats were struck Monday off the coast of the port city of Kargan and near Larak Island in Hormozgan province. Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor for security affairs, attributed the strike to the U.S. military. Nafisi said an unspecified number of fishermen were missing and that search-and-rescue operations were underway, according to Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the IRGC used the boats to try to capture a naval drone that the U.S. military uses to patrol the Strait of Hormuz. After U.S. forces identified the attempt, an American drone fired two missiles at the boats, destroying them and killing most of those on board. What they are saying: U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure, saying "Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a U.S. unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after CENTCOM forcefully responded." "The surface drone remains under U.S. operational control," Hawkins said. State of play: The incident took place as the U.S. attempts to protect increased commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil flows remain below prewar levels. A U.S. official said the U.S. military and Gulf countries have begun conducting daytime transits of tankers through the strait and not only night time as was the case in recent month. As fighting with the Houthis in the Red Sea escalates, Saudi Arabia has significantly increased the number of oil tankers it sends through the strait, a U.S. official said. U.S. forces have also expanded the mine-cleared parts of the strait's middle shipping lane. By the numbers: An average of 40 ships now transit the strait daily under U.S. military guidance and protection. Roughly 14 million barrels of oil are exported through the waterway daily, a U.S. official said. Over the last week, several tankers carrying liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas have also transited the strait.

Plans to build a new data centre could threaten the habitat of one of Britain's most endangered plants and a rare species of bumblebee, a wildlife trust said.
A planning application has already been submitted for the Google data centre at Arena Essex Raceway in Thurrock, which is designated as a local wildlife site.
It is home to the rare broad-leaved cudweed and shrill carder bumblebee and the Essex Wildlife Trust fears "incredibly rare" habitats would be "destroyed".
A Google spokesperson said it took "our environmental responsibilities very seriously".
Data centres are giant warehouses full of powerful computers used to run digital services, such as movie streaming, online banking and artificial intelligence.
There are 568 data centres listed in the UK, according to the data centre map., external
Emily Buttress, from the Essex Wildlife Trust, said her team was worried about the water and energy usage required, the warming effect on the surrounding land, and a lack of research about the long-term impacts of these buildings.
"We are quite worried with the rapid development of data centres," she said.
"What would it do for the local community in a water drought county? We are not against development, but it has to happen sustainably."
The Arena Essex Raceway announced in 2018 that it would stop hosting speedway fixtures for the Lakeside Hammers team.
Meanwhile, the Essex Wildlife Trust says the surrounding grassland and woodland has become home to 687 invertebrate and 439 plant species.
The trust said this included dingy skipper, which is a small moth-like butterfly, and the shrill carder bumblebee, which was only found in two areas in England.
It was designated as a local wildlife site in 2006. This does not offer legal protection from development, but it means council planners expect developers to look after the ecology.
Nightingale birds, the brown-banded carder bee and the five-banded weevil-wasp have also been recorded at the site.
But Global Infrastructure UK Limited bought the 129-acre (52-hectare) site in July 2023 for Â£47m (exclusive of VAT).
It submitted plans for the data centre on behalf of Google last year, and as part of the application, consultancy firm Mallory Land Ltd said the proposals took into account the ecology there.
In a statement submitted as part of the plans, Mallory Land Ltd said: "The demand for data centres has expanded significantly in recent years, driven by exponential growth in digital services, the emergence of artificial intelligence, cloud-based technologies, and the increasing adoption of smart infrastructure."
Google said data centres were vital to the UK economy and for online services.
"We share the Essex Wildlife Trust and Buglife's, external view that development at the former Arena Essex site must be sustainable," a spokesperson said.
"Our goal is to regenerate the site, bringing long-term investment and jobs to Thurrock while taking our environmental responsibilities very seriously."
The company had worked closely with Natural England and ecologists, they added, to "guarantee a 10% biodiversity net gain", "as well as ensuring a substantial part of the site is preserved for new public open space, green links, retained habitat, and the long-term enhancement of key woodland corridors".

The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.
Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?
Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches.
As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.
Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
"Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.
"Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.
"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says.
"From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse."
He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers".

10218e291961.text: By — Collin Binkley, Associated Press Collin Binkley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-first-lady-melania-trump-visits-north-carolina-school-to-discuss-tech-in-the-classroom Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: First lady Melania Trump visits North Carolina school to discuss tech in the classroom Politics Sep 15, 2026 10:12 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — First lady Melania Trump is set to visit northwestern North Carolina on Tuesday to talk to elementary school students, teachers and staff about how they're using technology in the classroom. Philip Landrigan learned about the attacks on 9/11 the way much of the world did when he was chair of the Department of Preventive Medicine at Mount Sinai School of Medicine in New York: by watching television.
“We were distressed that it was a terrorist attack,” he said in an interview on Friday, the 25th anniversary, “but our primary response was to be doctors.”
Mount Sinai, several miles uptown from the World Trade Center, did not immediately receive injured people, most of whom were taken to hospitals in lower Manhattan. Still, the hospital prepared. Surgeons finished the operations already underway but did not begin new ones, leaving operating rooms empty and ready for casualties.
Usually, when a disaster like this happens, there is a small number of deaths and a large number of injured people, Landrigan said. “But after the World Trade Center, it was the other way around.”
Landrigan and a group of doctors trained in occupational medicine began preparing for a different kind of patient. They quickly drafted a plan for evaluating workers who had been exposed to the cloud of dust that engulfed lower Manhattan after the towers collapsed, putting out the word through the media and major labor unions.
“We knew how to evaluate workers who had sustained hazardous exposure,” Landrigan said.
In the years that followed, the health consequences of 9/11 exposures would become increasingly clear.
Now, 25 years after the attacks, a trove of newly released city records and a new medical paper are shedding further light on what officials knew about the hazards in the aftermath of 9/11 and what researchers have since learned about their long-term health effects.
Last Wednesday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released 170,000 pages of records detailing health concerns, air-quality monitoring and correspondence among city officials during and after the attacks.
The documents, which had been stored in 68 boxes in a city office, offer a window into how officials grappled with the potential dangers as New Yorkers returned to lower Manhattan. At the time, city officials sought to reassure New Yorkers, assurances Landrigan said were overstated.
The day after Mamdani released the records, a paper published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, “Twenty-Five Years After 9/11—Lessons From the World Trade Center Health Program,” examined the long-term and evolving health effects linked to 9/11, some of which can emerge decades after exposure.
The authors drew on substantial research and data from the World Trade Center Health Program, the federal initiative that provides monitoring and treatment to eligible responders and survivors.
“This paper confirms and extends what we already knew about the hazards of the dust, and it shows that the political leaders at the time were not being honest when they told people that the air was safe,” said Landrigan, now director of the Global Observatory on Planetary Health at Boston College and not involved in the research.
“They were just trying to rally the population to tell people to be courageous, and I can sympathize with that,” he said. “The other motive, I think, was not so noble—they wanted to keep Wall Street going.”
The paper, by Alejandro Azofeifa and other scientists from the World Trade Center Health Program, found that those long-term consequences associated with the 9/11 attacks would take years to emerge. “Disaster-related health effects are often chronic, dynamic and involve multiple organs in the body,” Azofeifa said in an interview.
The first signs of harm, however, appeared much sooner.
Landrigan said he remembers the first workers who came in, a few days after the attacks, with what experts called the World Trade Center cough. “We made the link almost immediately.”
“I think the single most irritating component of the dust that was responsible for the cough was the pulverized cement,” he said.
To treat those patients, doctors initially focused on their symptoms, prescribing medications to relieve persistent coughs and other respiratory problems.
For a handful of patients, doctors performed bronchoscopies, passing a tube into the lungs.
Other illnesses materialized later. The new paper describes how cancer, respiratory disease and mental health conditions are among those with the strongest and longest-standing evidence linking them to 9/11 exposures.
For example, cancers associated with high levels of asbestos exposure can take decades to develop, with incidence typically rising 20 to 25 years after exposure, according to Landrigan. That long latency period means some cases linked to 9/11 exposures may only now be emerging.
Landrigan said lymphoma was among the first cancers to appear. One component of the dust that may have contributed to lymphoma was the carcinogen benzene, released from the jet fuel of the planes that crashed into the towers, he said.
For many, those health effects from the aftermath of the attacks do not occur in isolation. As the exposed population ages, researchers are increasingly seeing people living with multiple chronic conditions at once, which can lead to greater disability and make their medical care more complex.

The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry.
Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of which 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto.
Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology.
But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system.
Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle.
The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets.
Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch.
Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade.
Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus.
For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14.
The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research.
Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070.
Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency".
In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating.
The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates.
Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children.
While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown.
When Japan began its centenarian survey in 1963, there were 153 people aged 100 or over. That figure rose to 1,000 in 1981 and stood at 10,000 by 1998.
The most recent figures were released ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government honours those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup.
Studies have previously cast doubt on the validity of global centenarian numbers, suggesting data errors, unreliable public records and missing birth certificates may account for elevated figures.
A government audit of family registries in Japan in 2010 uncovered more than 230,000 people listed as being aged 100 or older who were unaccounted for, some having died decades previously.
The miscounting was attributed to patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" for some of the world's largest investors to spend their money in an era of geopolitical and economic uncertainty.
The country is "perfectly situated to build in the new global economic order", he told more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives gathered in Toronto for a major investment summit.
The group represent more than C$120tn ($86tn; Â£64tn) of assets. Carney's ambition is that they will invest in sectors like defence, energy, mining, AI and infrastructure.
Ottawa hopes they can be sold on more than 160 projects, from data centres to pipelines, and help Canada weather its trade war with the US.
Canada's dispute with its largest trade partner has prompted Carney to look to expand economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East as he seeks to reduce his country's reliance on its neighbour to the south.
"Our goal is simple: to make Canada the most attractive place in the G7 to invest," Carney said on Tuesday morning.
As part of that move, Carney announced plans to privatise operations for four of the country's largest airports, saying it would raise billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transport infrastructure.
Many of the business leaders attending the event in Toronto received a personal invitation from the prime minister, who worked in the top tiers of global finance and was a central banker before turning to politics.
Much of the action will take place in private sessions and bilateral meetings over the course of the day.
There will, however, be panels with speakers including Deutsche Bank AG CEO Christian Sewing, Bombardier executive Eric Martel, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.
The prime minister's office has played down the likelihood of any major announcements coming from the summit, with Carney saying over the weekend it was chance for deep-pocketed financiers to "come to 'peer into our shop window'".
The event is also an opportunity for Canada to burnish its reputation as a good place to do business after years of lagging investment performance.
Economic analysts say Canada needs to make significant policy changes to help attract investment, including more competitive tax and regulatory systems, and ensuring a supply of skilled labour.
For Carney, the event will be a test of whether he can deliver on his promise to strengthen the country's economic resilience.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month and the two countries have since imposed tit-for-tat tariffs.
On Tuesday, new US tariffs came into effect on a number of Canadian goods while some others were lifted, and bans on goods like alcohol and motorcycles are due to come into force next week.
On Tuesday, Carney addressed the American executives in Toronto directly.
"To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said.
"After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties."
Meanwhile, protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of organising a "great Canadian sell-off" of public resources and infrastructure to corporate interests, and hundreds appeared outside the opening night gala at a downtown museum.
"Half the buyers that he has invited here to Toronto are American," said Kai Nagata, with advocacy group Dogwood, on Monday.
"Let's be clear, every piece of our country that we sell off to American billionaires brings us closer to becoming the 51st state."
