The US Federal Reserve is likely to raise rates today, a move that many economists say is necessary to corral inflation, but which will put the central bankâs chair in conflict with the White House. The expected quarter-percentage-point hike is one of at least four that traders are betting on over the next year, with ING researchers arguing a 50-basis-point increase could actually be a better move today were it not for the inevitable political fallout.
US President Donald Trump has persistently argued â as recently as Sunday â that borrowing costs should fall rather than rise, despite analysts warning that energy price increases stemming from the Iran war threaten to push inflation, already above the Fedâs target, up further.

e09cb415b8fd.text:
Senior European business and political leaders hardened their stance towards China, suggesting a trade war between the two giant economies may be imminent.
Germanyâs chancellor said this week that Europeâs biggest economy supported tougher measures to combat âunfairâ Chinese trade practices, the CEO of Danish wind farm developer Ãrsted called for the EU to be âmuch more activeâ in supporting European industry against rivals from China, and the European Commission president said Brussels would use all means at its disposal to reduce what had become an âunsustainableâ trade deficit with Beijing. âThe EU would prefer to avoid a trade war with China,â a leading analyst of the two sidesâ relations wrote. âBut it may have no choice.â

1fe80741f6fc.text:
Tech leaders took opposing positions on regulating AI, pointing to a growing rift in the industry. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman â who last week called for not only US regulation, but also for a compact between Washington and Beijing â said his firm was collaborating with Anthropic and Google as they look to contain fears surrounding the technology.
However, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sided with Metaâs chief in rejecting calls for coordinating an AI slowdown, saying there was no need for regulation on AI safety. Experts fear the window for regulation in the US is closing fast ahead of midterm elections, which risk interrupting the momentum sparked by a researcherâs warning that advanced AI is spiraling out of control.

9ef7010693d8.text:
The Democratic Republic of Congo sought to speed up the implementation of a strategic mining partnership with the US, which is looking to rival Chinaâs influence in Africa. The DRC, the worldâs largest producer of cobalt, a key component in electronics, has already received US investment under the agreement as it seeks to attract more Western funds.
If Washingtonâs plan is fully realized, Congolese minerals will flow west on a US-backed rail line to a port in Angola and then onward to the US. Though China remains by far the biggest investor in African mining, countries across the continent are looking to reduce their reliance on Beijing while expanding their control over more valuable sections of the supply chain.

c5a76f545975.text:
The European Commission president invited Canada to become the EUâs first-ever âassociate member,â highlighting the global geopolitical realignment underway as a result of US pressure on allies. The move would transform the EU from a bloc defined by geography to one driven, at least ostensibly, by values.
It also risks further worsening Brusselsâ and Ottawaâs relations with Washington: US President Donald Trump has railed against both, and is locked in a trade war with the latter; several EU member states are reportedly wary of the White Houseâs reaction. Still, the announcement could transform the EU and set the stage for more geographically ambitious expansion: âWe are on the same page [as Canada],â Australiaâs trade minister told the Sydney Morning Herald.

444d1f9b4cd4.text:
The News
Somalilandâs president is putting almost everything on the table in his campaign to win US recognition for the breakaway territory of Somalia, offering US investors access to a strategically located port and mineral resources while leaving open the possibility of expanded military access.
âWe are not giving anything for free,â Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi âIrroâ said in an interview with Semafor in Washington. âWe have to offer something. And we expect the other partner [to have] the same or equal opportunities.â
Recognition is the prize, but economic cooperation, trade and investment can proceed in parallel. Somaliland can offer âour facilities and our minerals,â he said.
The US already has a military relationship with Somaliland, including training and security cooperation, but no military base there. The head of US Africa Command visited Hargeisa and Berbera last year as Washington continued to assess the territoryâs strategic importance.
Irro is signaling that the relationship could go further. Military access for the US, Israel or other countries, he said, âis a negotiation.â
âI will not rule out,â he said of a future base agreement, arguing that any deal would depend on what Somaliland receives in return, including greater security and support for its forces.
Yinkaâs view
Israelâs recognition in December changed the diplomatic equation on Somalilandâs status. It gave the breakaway territory its first recognition from a UN member state and, more importantly, demonstrated that the decades-old consensus against recognizing the territory could be broken.
Irro is now trying to turn that breakthrough into momentum. He is spending this week in Washington pressing his case at the White House and on Capitol Hill before heading to New York, where he hopes to meet other world leaders during the UN General Assembly and make the case for recognition.
The US is the next prize. Irro described America as the âbig fishâ Somaliland wants to pursue. âThe earlier, the better is always better,â he said.
His appeal is also tailored to Trump. Somaliland could name Berberaâs airport after him, Irro suggested, or welcome him to build a Trump Tower in Hargeisa.
The message underneath the flattery is more consequential since Somaliland is no longer simply making a historical or moral case for recognition. Irro is trying to show Washington what recognition could buy.
Room for Disagreement
Somalia sees the proposition very differently. Mogadishu rejects Somalilandâs claim to sovereignty and considers Berbera, its coastline and its resources part of Somalia.
That makes Irroâs offer of strategic and commercial access politically contested before any foreign government or company accepts it. Israelâs recognition has sharpened that dispute, turning Somalilandâs push for wider recognition into a more consequential challenge to Somaliaâs territorial claims.
Know More
Geography is central to Irroâs proposition. Berbera sits on the Gulf of Aden, close to the Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow maritime gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. As conflict and disruption have put renewed pressure on the regionâs sea lanes, Somaliland sees an opportunity to turn its location into diplomatic leverage.
Diego Garcia, the US military facility in the central Indian Ocean, lies thousands of kilometers away from the Red Sea theater. Berbera offers a far closer location for logistics, resupply or other military operations around the Gulf of Aden and Bab el-Mandab, even if it would not simply replace the much larger US presence on Diego Garcia.
Irro argued that American officials understand that strategic case. âThey know that,â he said, pointing to US training and security cooperation already taking place in Somaliland.
His offer is deliberately open-ended. Somaliland is not announcing a new US base; it is signaling that greater access could be negotiated. âWe are not giving anything for free,â Irro said, returning to the transactional logic behind his recognition campaign.
Step Back
Irro is also trying to sell Somaliland as an economic opportunity rather than simply a strategic outpost.
He points to Berberaâs port and free zone, an 850-kilometer coastline, fisheries and potentially significant oil, gas and mineral resources. Somalilandâs government budget has risen from less than $50 million when he became parliament speaker in 2005 to about $500 million today, he said.
The ambition is considerably bigger. Irro said Somaliland could be âvery richâ within a decade and claimed its budget could eventually reach $3 billion-$4 billion a year if its marine economy and other resources are developed.
Recognition, in his view, would help unlock that potential by making it easier for US and other international investors to treat Somaliland as a conventional investment destination rather than an unrecognized territory.
The View From China
Irroâs push for US recognition does not mean he wants Somaliland locked into a single geopolitical camp.
Taiwanâs representative office will remain in Hargeisa despite Beijingâs opposition. âWe have decided Taiwan to remain,â Irro said, noting that Taiwan was already present when he took office.
China is still welcome to invest. âIf China is coming without condition, we will welcome China,â he said. Chinese companies already operate in Somaliland, he added.
The line Irro draws is political saying no foreign power will decide Somalilandâs diplomatic relationships. âNobody can dictate to us,â he said.

- Published
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity.
He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs, which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily.
The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt with no tie on Wednesday, the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago.
Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and subsequently skipped multiple hearings.
The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial.
The first trial date is scheduled in November.
The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy.
The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, to 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC.
Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes has told the court his client suffers from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise.
In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election.
Duterte heads to trial at the ICC as his family is caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos.
The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025.
Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term.
But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial, where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office.
She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated.

- Published
Surrey Wildlife Trust has introduced 30 nationally-endangered water voles to a nature reserve near Elstead.
The release on the River Wey comes following a "successful" release on the upper river.
The water voles are being introduced downstream on 10 sites between Frensham and Elstead, the wildlife trust said.
James Herd, director of reserves management at the trust, said: "As we work towards the restoration of natural ecosystems and landscapes county wide, I hope this release is one of many reintroductions of native species that we'll see in the years ahead."
Water voles have been functionally extinct in Surrey since the early 2000s, but co-ordinated reintroduction and habitat improvement efforts by nature restoration groups are working to help the endearing species thrive again.
The trust said in a statement that it hoped that over the coming months, the aquatic rodents will "adapt easily to life on the 16-hectare reserve at Thundry Meadows and establish widely across the top of the Wey catchment".
Their return would also benefit other species which depend on healthy wetland habitats including herons and birds of prey, they added.
David Elliott, National Trust lead ranger for the South Downs West said: "Nature wins when we work together."
"It's so encouraging to see the water voles returning after all this time, they have been locally extinct for decades.
"The return of this enchanting species adds a missing piece to this jigsaw."
The release is part of a wider effort led by the National Trust, River Wey Trust and South East Rivers Trust to reintroduce the locally extinct species back to the River Wey.

46855d867c82.text:
Jasonâs view
On September 15, Saudi Arabia issued alerts for Mecca, Jeddah, and Taif. They were soon lifted and no impact was reported. The threat came after the Houthis, the Iranian-backed militia controlling northern Yemen, swept down Yemenâs Red Sea coast.
They took Mokha, a port city near the coastâs southern end, and Mayun, an island in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and then moved to the Hanish islands to the north. The Houthis now hold nearly the entire Yemeni side of one of the worldâs most important shipping lanes and sit roughly 20 miles from the main American military base in Africa, in Djibouti.
When I served as the White House Middle East envoy, the Houthis were not my file, but they were never far from it. Few governments treated them as a serious actor. They were seen as a ragtag militia, a Saudi and Emirati problem, and a humanitarian story. Itâs true that the group isnât an impressive military, but they hold Yemenâs capital, the part of the country where most Yemenis live, and now nearly all of its Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE recognized the danger early and fought the Houthis for years. That coalition frayed: the UAE drew down its forces in 2019, a UN-brokered truce largely halted the war in 2022, and Riyadh resumed direct talks with the Houthis.
The Houthis are a US-designated terror proxy of the Iranian regime. Their rule in Yemen has inflicted suffering on people through corruption, coercion, aid diversion, and war. Their latest offensive reportedly came with direct guidance from Tehran. According to Reuters, Tehran instructed the Houthis to escalate, promising them more money, weapons, and expert Iranian advisers.
The reason behind the timing is clear. For more than six months the US has been raising the cost to Iran of using the Strait of Hormuz as a weapon, and Iran has answered by putting another global energy chokepoint under threat. A drone strike that Riyadh attributes to an Iran-aligned group in Iraq also shut down the pipeline carrying Saudi oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz.
The Houthis have been hard to stop for reasons that have nothing to do with their quality as soldiers. They fight with cheap drones and missiles against interceptors that can cost a thousand times as much. From mountain strongholds, they have survived years of Saudi-led airstrikes and, more recently, American and British ones. Iranian weapons keep reaching them despite an air and sea blockade. Most of all, no campaign against them has been sustained. Each stopped before it was finished.
This time could be different. The Houthi advance gave their enemies a new set of exposed fixed targets. A militia holding a port city, an airfield, islands, and a long stretch of coastline can be found and hit. The Houthis wanted that ground because it brings their weapons closer to the ships they want to threaten, but holding it also puts them out in the open. This opportunity will not last long as they move to fortify these new coastal positions.
The countries with the most to gain from acting now were together in one room last week. United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed that Admiral Brad Cooper hosted senior military leaders from eight nations in Germany to discuss regional security cooperation. According to reports, they represented Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt.
Six years ago, the Abraham Accords that US President Donald Trump created brought Israel into open partnership with the UAE and Bahrain, clearing the way for the Pentagon to move Israel under CENTCOMâs umbrella alongside its Arab neighbors. Military relationships that began with missile defense have grown into a room where Israel and seven Arab states, most of them not party to the accords, strategize against a shared threat. According to Axios, Cooper told the group that American forces are staying in the Middle East, and discussions are underway about extending to Saudi Arabia the intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance support that Israel already provides to the UAE.
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a Houthi drone headed toward Mecca, and the Houthis deny it. Whatever the truth of the September 15 alerts, Tehran understands what a threat to Islamâs holiest city does to Sunni opinion while its Shia proxy attacks Saudi Arabia. Iran seeks regional dominance by setting Muslim against Muslim, country against country, and everyone against Israel. To some degree, its pressure is producing the opposite. Regional countries are increasingly coordinating against Iran and its proxies, building a habit of cooperation that will ultimately lead to normalization.
Taking the Houthis head-on requires sustained strikes on their new coastal positions, a joint maritime mission aimed at Iranian resupply, and a declared goal of removing the Houthis from the Red Sea coast, not managing them there.
For years the Houthis were dismissed as a nuisance. They now threaten one of the worldâs most important oil routes while their patron in Tehran squeezes another. This is the moment for the Gulf states, the US, Israel, and their allies to take advantage of a ripe opportunity to act together. Waiting is how the Houthis got this far.
Jason D. Greenblatt served as White House Middle East Envoy in the first Trump administration. He is the author of In the Path of Abraham, the founder of Abraham Venture LLC, and publishes the Substack âHow to Watchâ
Notable
- Saudi Arabiaâs crown prince traveled to Egypt to meet President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi, who commands the Arab worldâs largest military. The kingdom is reluctant to act alone against the Houthis, Bloomberg reported.

7df50aa57021.text: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades. The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said. Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation. The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities. Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable." Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order. "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios. His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users. The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens. What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants. Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating. Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

- Published
A wildlife trust has called for a new offshore disposal site to be found for sediment dredged from Brighton Marina, saying it remains concerned about plans being explored off Newhaven.
Brighton Marina has been looking for a long-term disposal site since Sussex Wildlife Trust successfully challenged a licence in 2025 for disposal of sediment at Rottingdean.
The marina has said dredging is needed to maintain safe access and there are limited options available for disposal sites.
Sussex Wildlife Trust said Newhaven was a "protected area" that sat adjacent to the Beachy Head West Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ).
Campaigners previously claimed the silt was a "black, thick, slimy, petrochemically smelling sludge", but Premier Marinas, which owns Brighton Marina, said dredged silt was regularly sampled to confirm it was not harmful.
John Cervenka, Premier Marinas chief operating officer, said: "Maintaining safe navigational access to Brighton Marina is not optional. It is a legal requirement and fundamental to the operation of the marina."
He said the marina was a major centre of economic activity.
According to the marina, about 150 businesses depend on the site, creating jobs for about 1,200 people, with more than eight million visits each year.
Premier Marinas said Newhaven had been identified as a potential alternative by Sussex Wildlife Trust.
However, the trust said in a statement on social media, external: "We have not promoted or endorsed Newhaven over any other option."
The trust said: "Newhaven sits adjacent to Beachy Head West MCZ, and we remain concerned about potential impacts on this protected area.
"Our preferred option is a new offshore disposal site, well away from the MCZ."
The trust said that Newhaven was already used for dredge disposal by Newhaven Port, and there was currently no available data on the impacts of additional disposal there.
Until it saw further evidence, it did not have a view on whether Newhaven was suitable, it added.
"We will respond to any future licence application based on the ecological evidence it contains," it said.
Brighton Marina hopes to submit a marine licence application to the Marine Management Organisation in November.
If approved, maintenance dredging could restart next spring.

33f760c77d2d.text:
WhatsApp groups and social media across Saudi Arabia lit up on Tuesday with variations of the same message: The Houthis are attacking Mecca. Photos of the Kaaba and prayers of âGod protect this countryâ spread after Saudi civil defense issued an alert for Islamâs holiest city, the first since the war began, before lifting it minutes later. Some questioned whether it was an error or a test, while others condemned their âfellow Muslimsâ for threatening what is holy.
Over the past six months, there was a sense that Mecca would provide a shield for western Saudi Arabia. As sirens went off over Riyadh and the Eastern Province, people in the Hejaz assumed no one would dare approach what all Muslims deem sacred. Tuesdayâs alert punctured that logic. While nothing was hit â Saudi authorities said a drone was intercepted â the taboo has been broken. Nothing is holy in war.

Gulf airlines are coming out swinging after a brutal year, fending off opportunistic European rivals and instability at home. Nowhere is this clearer than in Dammam, where Saudi Arabia has ordered a new budget airline and an expansion of King Fahd International Airport. Run by an Air Arabia-led consortium, it will fly Airbus A320s on domestic routes to Riyadh, Jeddah, and Madinah.
In long-haul, Emirates won a coveted Berlin slot this week, strengthening its Europe-Asia foothold. Some European airlines have opened new Middle Eastern routes this year, which Emirates President Tim Clark called âa little bit sad,â and an attempt to exploit the Iran war. The Dubai carrier expects to restore full prewar seat capacity by the end of 2026, returning âhard and fastâ if the conflict subsides. Abu Dhabiâs Etihad is taking the same muscular approach, adding more than 20 aircraft and new routes to Europe, Africa, and China as other long-haul carriers have pulled back.

10ec6ef92d04.text: Kristen Silverberg, a widely respected policy expert and former ambassador, was named the new president and CEO of Business Roundtable , the top policy voice of America's leading CEOs. Silverberg, now BRT's president and chief operating officer, will succeed Josh Bolten , a former White House chief of staff who has led the organization for the past decade , when he steps down on Jan. 31. Why it matters: Business Roundtable is one of Washington's most influential associations. The 200+ members are CEOs of the biggest U.S.-based companies, most with global reach. The CEOs use BRT to amplify what they consider the most important messages business leaders can deliver to government. Silverberg — who worked with Bolten in the White House and is a former U.S. ambassador to the European Union from 2008 to 2009 — said in a statement that a key mission of BRT, American companies and their CEOs is championing and delivering growth and jobs. "The American economy is undergoing a profound transformation," she said. "Leaders in government and business have an extraordinary opportunity and a responsibility to strengthen American growth and competitiveness while expanding opportunity for workers and communities." "Business Roundtable has a critical role to play in advancing policies that make America the best place in the world to build, grow and invest in a business." The backstory: Silverberg, 55, was an assistant secretary of State under President George W. Bush and was a law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and Judge David Sentelle of the U.S. Court of Appeals. She's a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Texas School of Law. What they're saying: BRT chair Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco Systems, called Silverberg a "proven and strategic leader, with the deep trust and respect of Business Roundtable's Board and members." "Kristen has been instrumental in positioning the organization and its leaders as effective advocates for policies that help American businesses grow and innovate while expanding opportunity for workers and communities across the country." Bolten told me in an interview: "Kristen Silverberg is one of the finest policy professionals in America today. Over the last several years, she earned broad respect among Business Roundtable members and the enthusiastic support of BRT's board. "I could not be happier that they have selected Kristen to lead BRT through the challenging years ahead." What's next: Bolten, already a member of several major boards, plans a "portfolio" approach for his next phase. 🏟️ On his bucket list: visiting all 30 Major League Baseball ballparks with his son.

4df8f203f22c.text:
Destructive immune cells tied to Alzheimer’s disease may get their marching orders from cells outside the brain rather than within it.
In mice, suppressing a small population of immune cells located in lymph nodes protects against neurodegeneration, researchers report September 3 in Nature Neuroscience. The findings raise the possibility of treating Alzheimer’s disease while bypassing the brain’s siege defenses.
For years, researchers have gone all in on efforts to remove toxic tangles of proteins like amyloid and tau from the brain as a way of halting Alzheimer’s, with limited success. But the immune system also plays an important role in neurodegeneration. What exactly that role is — protector or antagonist — has been unclear.
In 2023, neurologist David Holtzman and colleagues showed that immune system T cells accumulate around tau tangles — implying that they might cause damage. Halting these cells’ entry into the brain reduced inflammation, and also reduced neuronal damage, says Holtzman, of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.
Still, it wasn’t known how these T cells accessed the brain in the first place. “A big question has been whether the T cells passively enter the brain or are primed … to do so,” says Rudolph Tanzi, a neurogeneticist at Harvard Medical School who wasn’t involved in the study.
During priming, T cells are ordered to rally and multiply. The generals that bark out these orders are called dendritic cells, which capture signatures of cellular threats called antigens and present them to T cell infantry.
No one had looked closely at what dendritic cells in lymph nodes were doing during neurodegenerative disease, Holtzman says. So in the new study, he and his colleagues compared two groups of mice engineered to have tau-linked neurodegeneration, one of which lacked dendritic cells.
Blocking an attack
Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration can ravage a brain, as seen in the slice of a mouse’s brain at left. The attack may be planned in the lymph nodes, new research suggests. The brain slice depicted on the right came from a mouse in which that early stage of attack was blocked.
In old age, mice without dendritic cells still had brains packed with tau. But compared with the other mice, they were protected against neurodegeneration and performed better on cognitive tasks like nest building.
They also had far fewer T cells in their brains. This suggests that tau tangles aren’t working alone in driving neurodegeneration, Holtzman says. “A lot of the damage that tau is causing is due to the inflammatory response that it’s eliciting.” The results would need to be replicated in human brains, he adds.
Despite this seemingly important role, the researchers found few dendritic cells in the mice’s brains. Instead, they detected threat-mimicking brain proteins traveling to the lymph nodes, where dendritic cells used them to rally T cells. The team bred mutant mice with demoted dendritic cell generals that could no longer give commands to T cells. These mice also had fewer T cells in their brains and better-preserved brain structures.
It isn’t practical to disable dendritic cells from birth in people at risk of Alzheimer’s. But Holtzman says his colleagues are working on cellular targets that could suppress them in adulthood. The real promise of the study may be a dementia treatment that bypasses the nervous system’s locked vault — the blood-brain barrier, Holtzman says. “If this panned out, potentially you wouldn’t have to get [therapeutics] into the brain.”

eefa4f4096bb.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-dr-nicole-saphier-testifies-in-confirmation-hearing-for-u-s-surgeon-general Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Dr. Nicole Saphier testifies in confirmation hearing for U.S. surgeon general Politics Sep 16, 2026 10:06 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Dr. Nicole Saphier, President Donald Trump's third nominee to serve as surgeon general, will face lawmakers at her confirmation hearing Wednesday in the latest attempt to fill the post known as the nation's doctor. The hearing begins at 10 a.m. EDT. Watch live in the video player above. Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News Channel contributor, is Trump's newest pick after entrepreneur and wellness influencer Dr. Casey Means saw her path forward stall in the Senate over her background and vaccine views. Trump withdrew his first nominee, Fox News medical contributor Janette Nesheiwat, after questions arose about her academic credentials. READ MORE: Trump pulls Casey Means' stalled surgeon general nomination, picks Nicole Saphier instead Saphier will face questions from the Senate health committee for a position that carries limited policymaking power but a loud megaphone as the nation's top communicator with Americans on public health issues. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. While senators may scrutinize her credentials and background, Saphier will also be in the difficult position of navigating Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s more contentious policies, including his efforts to scale back vaccine guidance when measles outbreaks around the country are alarming the medical community. Lawmakers of both parties have criticized Kennedy's stances and are likely to grill Saphier over whether she'll more fiercely advocate vaccination if confirmed. Saphier is director of breast imaging at Memorial Sloan Kettering Monmouth, according to her profile on the New York-based institution's website. She has a doctor of medicine degree from Ross University School of Medicine in Barbados along with fellowships at the Mayo Clinic, the profile said. Like Means, who is a close Kennedy ally, Saphier has questioned whether every child needs to get the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, a longtime recommendation that the Trump administration has been trying to weaken. Saphier has, however, disagreed with Trump and Kennedy on some issues, telling The Associated Press last fall that Trump's cautions to pregnant women who take Tylenol were oversimplistic and "patronizing." Her latest ethics filing, dated Sept. 7, shows holdings with various healthcare and insurance firms, as well as processed food companies, like Coca-Cola, Yum Brands, the Hershey Co. and cigarette maker Philip Morris. Before entering politics and throughout his tenure at the health department, Kennedy has criticized big pharmaceutical companies and insurance firms for alleged corruption and decried ultraprocessed foods as contributing to a nationwide chronic disease crisis. Additionally, Saphier owns DropRx, a firm that produces controversial, unregulated tinctures — concentrated liquid extracts promoting focus and calm — that contain ingredients, including kava kava root, described by the FDA as potentially causing severe liver injury. Her filing says she will resign from her position with DropRx and Empower MD LLC, which owns DropRx, if she is confirmed. She states in the document that she would partially or fully divest from holdings that would present a conflict to serving as surgeon general. Also facing lawmakers' questions Wednesday is Chris Klomp, chief counselor of the Health and Human Services Department, who has been nominated to serve as Kennedy's second-in-command. Also at the hearing will be Timothy Westlake, chief of staff at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, who is seeking confirmation to be assistant secretary for mental health and substance use. Since the dawn of the Space Age, the weaponization of space has been an international concern. Now the United States has announced, with few details, that it has weapons in orbit.
“The United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending … against hostile adversary action,” U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said September 14 at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Md.
With such limited information, it’s hard to know what to make of the announcement. But “the world should be listening with open ears about this information because of the wide range of consequences,” says astrodynamicist Thomas González Roberts of Georgia Tech in Atlanta.
Space weapons are difficult to define and encompass many different possible technologies. “There’s real ambiguity about the term ‘space weapon,’” Roberts says. These weapons can involve satellites directly attacking other satellites, with projectiles, explosives, lasers or other methods. A satellite could physically grab and manipulate another satellite. Cyberattacks can incapacitate satellites or wrest control away from their operators. Space weapons could also affect life on the ground, for example, by disrupting GPS services.
And space weapons have a long history. In 1962, the United States tested a nuclear weapon at high altitude, which incapacitated many of the satellites orbiting at that time. Soon thereafter, the 1967 Outer Space Treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in space. (Although, recently, the United States has alleged that Russia is testing technology needed to put a nuclear weapon in orbit.)
Multiple nations, including the United States, have also tested antisatellite weapons that can take spacecraft down by launching weapons from the ground or air. Worryingly, some types of space weapons could make orbits unusable, by strewing dangerous debris that can collide with satellites or anything else in its path.
Science News spoke with Roberts about what we know and don’t know about the weapons Meink referred to. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
SN: What do we know about these space weapons?
Roberts: When I saw this news, my first take was that it’s missing a lot of adjectives. The way we describe a space weapon is by its method of attack and the consequences of using that weapon.
So when I think about what a space weapon is, I think about questions like is an attack attributable — can others see who did it? Is it reversible, meaning the effects on the target can be undone? And will there be public awareness about whether it was successful or not? Could the attacker themselves determine if it was successful or not?
And could there be collateral damage, meaning other satellites or other space assets would be damaged or degraded? This is what I’m curious about for these U.S. weapons.
So, what kind of weapon do I think it is? I think it’s one where the benefits in those categories are greatest.
SN: Could it be connected to plans for the Golden Dome missile defense system, which would put missile interceptors in orbit?
Roberts: I had the same thought. Could this be that? Could this be something different?
The hint [Meink gave] of “space control” as an adjective is bothersome to me. I want more information. Are we talking about affecting your adversary’s ability to control their satellites? Are you saying the capability is for the United States to control another satellite? The use of the word “control” really sparks my thought processes. There are weapons where you can steal control away from someone else: cyberattacks, grappling, noncooperative rendezvous and proximity operations. I don’t know what the statement means in this context.
SN: Should we be concerned about space debris if these weapons are used?
Roberts: Some space weapons produce collateral damage. A fragmentation event produces nondiscriminate debris, meaning debris that will run into you no matter what your nationality is. But many, many satellite attacks, you can easily focus them on just your target. I would imagine the U.S. is talking about that. The U.S. is the biggest actor in space. They can’t afford to jeopardize the environment.
SN: How could someone attack another satellite without producing debris?
Roberts: Jamming it is the best idea here. If you’re jamming the signals with which a satellite receives or sends data, that means it’s not useful to its operator. But that doesn’t mean that it’s dead.
A lot of these attacks are targeting certain subsystems. Shining a laser at a satellite is particularly damaging to an optical or infrared sensor. If you think a satellite is taking pictures of Earth, like any spy satellite or reconnaissance satellite, you might be interested in disabling just that optical sensor.
SN: What might the repercussions of this announcement be?
Roberts: It really invites criticism from U.S. adversaries. The global community has been working for some time on preventing an arms race in outer space. It offers evidence to some who might claim that it’s too late.
Right now, states obfuscate. There’s evidence for Russia and China developing space weapons, testing them and demonstrating them. But largely they deny it. In most cases, they pretend they’re not doing anything at all. And the U.S. is taking a different approach. Instead of obfuscating it, they’re telling everyone.

2da6e3c51116.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union's first "associate member." Why it matters: Canada and the EU are testing whether a nation deeply dependent on the U.S. market can find economic independence by moving closer to Europe. This could also present one of the most permanent effects of President Trump 's trade wars : U.S. allies building markets, supply chains and security ties designed to make them less vulnerable to Washington. If the proposal goes through, the shift would pull Ottawa deeper into Europe's economic and security architecture as Canada reduces its reliance on the U.S. — something Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has signaled the nation is open to . Driving the news: In her annual state of the union address, von der Leyen framed the Canada offer as part of Europe's response to a world where "old assumptions and relationships have frayed." Speaking directly to Carney, she said democracies "have the freedom to choose with whom to work." Her proposal would move beyond their existing trade pact to integrate their defense industries and deepen ties on manufacturing, technology, energy, and the Arctic. This comes after Trump has spent more than a year threatening Canada's economy and sovereignty , repeatedly calling for it to become the 51st state and imposing some of America's harshest tariffs. In addition to 50% tariffs, Trump will block certain Canadian dairy, alcohol and auto imports later this month. What they're not saying: The White House, the European Commission and the Canadian prime minister's office have not yet responded to requests for comment. Context: The EU already extends its single market without full membership to Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, but Canada's associate membership would likely differ. The single market guarantees the free movement of goods, services, capital and people, and it requires member states to accept Brussels' regulations. Canada already has a substantial free-trade deal with Europe that has eliminated tariffs on about 99% of goods, so the real question is whether associate membership will reach deeper into services, regulation, investment or coordination. Canadian exports to the U.S. dropped 5.8% last year while exports elsewhere jumped 17.2%, according to the Canadian government . But America still bought 71.7% of Canada's exports. The big picture: Canada offers critical assets both the U.S. and Brussels need. It is the world's fourth-largest oil producer , providing more oil to the U.S. than every other foreign supplier combined. It ranked among the world's top five producers of 11 critical minerals last year, according to Natural Resources Canada . Nearly half the country reaches into the Arctic, giving it strategic reach as melting ice opens new routes, Russia builds up its military and China grows its presence. Canada also brings a ready-made defense industry. It is the first non-European country in the EU's SAFE defense procurement program, giving Canadian companies a leg up on providing defense contracts. Between the lines: Canada is running an experiment other middle powers will watch: Can it replace its dependence on American markets? Trump has argued the trade war would revive American manufacturing. Yet manufacturing jobs have fallen since he took office last year, and Canada now buys less American goods , not more. What we don't know: Carney and von der Leyen haven't laid out what an associate membership would entail, including whether Canada would gain access to the single market, which EU rules it would have to follow, or whether Canadians and Europeans would gain rights to live, work or study across the Atlantic. What's next: Carney is expected to address the European Parliament on Thursday. Canada will then host the next Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30.

2307d338e4c2.text:
Scientists have made mice with a remarkable amount of room for human brain tissue to grow.
By genetically engineering animals lacking part of their brain, researchers created a living model in which pea-sized clumps of human neurons could expand, mature and wire into a developing nervous system, ultimately coming to dominate the mouse cortex, the brain’s outer layer.
The model offers a new way to study human neural circuits and brain disease, researchers report September 16 in Nature.
“Our goal has been to make aspects of human brain development and function accessible for investigation, so we can develop therapeutics,” says Sergiu Pașca, a neuroscientist at Stanford University.
The idea of growing miniature brain structures in a lab dish emerged in the early 2010s, when researchers in Austria showed that stem cells could self-organize into 3-D tissue resembling aspects of the developing human brain. But these tiny clusters of human nerve cells, called organoids, lacked the connections and sensory inputs of a living brain.
In 2022, Pașca and his colleagues developed a way to transplant human organoids into newborn rats, eventually getting the human cells to make up about one-third of one side of the rat’s cortex. But rat neurons mature faster than their human counterparts, capping how much the human tissue could develop in this rodent model.
Pașca and his colleagues bred mice genetically engineered to develop without most of their cortex and the neighboring hippocampus — two structures involved in movement, learning and memory that together account for about half of the brain’s total volume. Although the resulting animals showed some behavioral defects, they were “surprisingly functional,” Pașca says.
The cavernous space created by the missing tissue could then accommodate human brain organoids grown from healthy donor stem cells — a transplantation that successfully took hold in 25 of 29 attempts.
Over the next three months, the human tissue expanded nearly fivefold in volume in these mice, ultimately filling more than 90 percent of the cortex. The tissue developed into a range of cell types, including rare neurons that have proved nearly impossible to generate in a dish. The tissue lacked some features of a mature cortex, including its characteristic layers, yet still wired extensively into the mouse nervous system, providing a platform for studying human neural circuits gone awry.
The researchers used the mice to model cerebral palsy, a disability caused by damage to the developing brain. They subjected the grafted animals to oxygen deprivation. Afterward, the human tissue showed cellular signs of injury, and the mice developed problems with gait and limb coordination — features of the disability in people, too.
“This could be used down the line to test many therapeutics that are being considered for cerebral palsy,” Pașca says. He plans to study [frontotemporal] dementia and genetic forms of autism with the mice, using organoids made from patient-derived cells affected by those conditions.
The technique “is certainly bold,” says H. Isaac Chen, a neurosurgeon at the University of Pennsylvania who studies brain organoids but was not involved in the research. The extent of humanization raises questions about the ethical boundaries of such experiments, Chen notes, but Pașca has gone to unusual lengths to grapple with those concerns. “He has done a lot more than others in terms of not just holding these discussions but actually driving them,” Chen says.
Pașca, for example, consulted an outside panel of experts, led by Insoo Hyun, a bioethicist at the National University of Singapore Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine. Hyun acknowledges that this new mouse model raises legitimate questions about where to draw the ethical line, but says there is little evidence that these mice have crossed it.
What matters, he says, is not how much human tissue an animal contains, but what that tissue enables it to do. On tests of fine motor control and memory, the grafted mice’s performances fell somewhere between that of the mice with intact brains and those lacking a cortex. “From a secular ethical point of view,” Hyun says, “it boils down to cognitive capacity” — and so far, these mice don’t seem to have gained any obvious extra brainpower.
That may be a relief to anyone picturing the lab mice from Animaniacs, the genetically enhanced rodents who spend each night plotting to take over the world. In Pașca’s lab, there’s little evidence of any plans for world domination. His mice, despite their mostly human-derived cortex, remain far more Pinky than Brain.

The News
Rep. Kevin Kiley, I-Calif, said Wednesday he does not plan to caucus with Republicans next year if he is reelected to the House as an independent.
In an interview with Semaforâs Nicholas Wu at the Youth Wellbeing Forum, Kiley said he is working to change House rules that require independent members to affiliate with a party in order to sit on committees. He currently caucuses with Republicans for committee purposes.
âIâm an independent member now, and yet the rules of the House force me to say, okay, as a formality, for the purposes of committee assignments, Iâm in conference with one side or the other,â Kiley said during the joint interview with Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, D-Ore.
âThe committee seats should belong to the American people, and you shouldnât be denied a seat on committees just because youâre an independent member,â he added.
Know More
Wednesdayâs event in Washington also touched on a leadership contest among House Democrats on the Education and Workforce Committee, where Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-Conn., is challenging Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Va., for the top Democratic position on the House Education and Workforce Committee.
Asked whether she would take a side, Bonamici declined to back Scott saying âIâm just weighing my options right now and talking to people in the committee.â
Scott, who is 79 years old, has held the top committee role for six terms.
Bonamici may decide to run herself for the top Democratic slot on the panel, a person familiar with her thinking later told Semafor.
The lawmakers â both of whom are members of the House education panel â also discussed broader education policy goals.
Kiley criticized efforts by the Trump administration to dismantle the Department of Education, calling the move âfundamentally misguided.â
âWhen it comes to the core mission of supporting educational excellence across the country, to say that weâre just not going to have this done in the Department of Education anymore, and weâre going to send it to some other department makes absolutely no sense to me,â Kiley said.
Bonamici said she plans to introduce a bill as soon as Thursday aimed at updating federal education policy to better address the needs of todayâs students, including through project-based learning, arts education, and studentsâ behavioral health needs.
âOur education policy has not kept up with the needs of todayâs youth,â Bonamici said. âWe need a well-rounded education.â
Kiley discussed his work on the High-Quality Charter Schools Act, which would create a federal tax credit for charitable contributions to nonprofit charter-school organizations.
Nicholas Wu contributed reporting.

88709ffaff0c.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press By — Eddie Pells, Associated Press Eddie Pells, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-senate-meets-after-advancing-college-sports-act Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Senate meets after advancing College Sports Act Politics Sep 16, 2026 10:50 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A bill that proposes to fix some of the biggest problems in college sports — spiraling spending, constant lawsuits and a transfer portal run amok — cleared a major hurdle Tuesday when the Senate voted 74-24 to halt debate and move the measure one step closer to a final up-or-down vote. Watch the Senate floor live in the video player above. The Protect College Sports Act, a bill co-sponsor Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called "a bipartisan solution designed to bring order to the chaos" easily cleared the 60-vote threshold it needed to stop the filibuster. WATCH: Senate Democrats block cryptocurrency bill, demanding more limits on Trump's investments Co-sponsor Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said the lopsided nature of the vote left her "cautiously optimistic" it could get through the House, which has failed repeatedly in passing a different version of a college sports bill. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. There remains, however, a persistent block of opposition. "What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation," said Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn. Notably, all four Black Democrats in the Senate — Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Angela Alsobrooks — voted against the bill that is strongly opposed by the NAACP. The vote came a week after college football's most recent crisis — a scheduled meeting of school presidents in the Southeastern Conference to expel LSU over its now-canceled plans to place players on the roster who had participated in NFL training camps. READ MORE: Key Sens. Cruz, Cantwell look to break college sports logjam in Congress with a bipartisan bill Calmer heads prevailed. The eligibility lawsuit that triggered the mess is the sort of litigation the bill would outlaw. "That was probably like a big lamp for some people who saw it and said, 'Oh my God, this is so out of control,'" Cantwell said in an interview with The Associated Press. "You can see how out-of-hand the situation was getting." Introduced in May, compromises finally got the bill to the floor in September Cantwell and Cruz introduced the bill in late May and it nearly died without the support of the Southeastern and Big Ten conferences. Compromises helped get them on board, then it became a matter of getting the bill onto the floor of the busy upper chamber. At around the time the vote took place, Cantwell released a report that outlined a "spending spiral" that has taken hold of college sports since name-image-likeness payments began. Among its findings: There was a $519.9 million increase in institutional and government support of athletic programs between 2015 and 2025 among the 53 schools in the Power Four whose data was publicly available. The bill promises to harness that in a number of ways, including: Placing into law the 22% cap (around $21.5 million this year) on revenue colleges are allowed to share with their players — an amount agreed to in the House settlement that defined the rules over paying players. It would add a $27.5 million "retention pool" for schools to keep current players in a move that could bring some of the hard-to-regulate third-party NIL deals back in-house. Giving conferences the option of pooling their TV media rights, a move proponents say could raise between $4 billion and $8 billion in additional revenue. The SEC and Big Ten disagree and say they would not participate. Restricting players to one "free" transfer where they wouldn't have to sit out a year, which could limit bidding wars that take place year-round in the transfer portal. Placing into law the NCAA's new rule that allows players five years of eligibility, but no more. Critics say the NCAA, which has struggled to police its business for the last 100 years, shouldn't be getting more power. "Over and over again, courts have determined that colleges and the NCAA and conferences are violating the law," Murphy said. The bill, however, has gained support from a long list of sports leaders, including retired football coach Nick Saban and Deion Sanders of Colorado, and basketball coaches John Calipari of Arkansas and Mark Few of Gonzaga. "I think this clears up about 75-80% of our issues," Calipari said at a news conference in Washington on Monday, the eve of the vote. "Nothing is perfect. This is a bite out of the apple." There's a last-minute push before the elections Though the bill passed on a bipartisan measure, some lawmakers view it as their best chance to do something with the uncertainty of the upcoming election looming. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber. Democrats are trying to flip the Senate in November's midterms, which can complicate the legislative agenda. "We're going to get one shot at this, and I don't know if we ever will again soon," said another co-sponsor, Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., just ahead of the vote. "We've got a moment." The bill, he said, could "define the trajectory of college athletics." Pells reported from Denver. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.
The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening âand taking political action, not in debates âover personnel".
Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability.
He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership.
Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September.
The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state.
It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government.
Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers.
The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims.
The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU.
The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, â Germany's political landscape needs stability".
"Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia.
It comes after Markus SÃ¶der, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz.
An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses.
However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls.
In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority.
The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament.
Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely.
No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including SÃ¶der, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik WÃ¼st and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors.
Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive â¬500bn ($547bn; Â£420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage.
But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany.
This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted.

The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe.
In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ charged five men allegedly connected to the Russian Intelligence Services (RIS). The men are accused of paying, or trying to pay, people in the US and overseas to target those "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine".
"It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche. All those accused remain at large.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday Moscow will not comment until it hears or sees "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".
It is not clear if the five accused are in the United States, or in a different location.
Washington has charged all five men with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum 20-year prison sentence.
Three of the defendants are "high-ranking members of the RIS network", the DoJ said.
Among them are Russian father and son Yuri Khrameev, 63, and Kirill Khrameev, 27. Khrameev senior was a colonel in the Russian intelligence services and his son is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia (FSB).
The third high-ranking suspect is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban national who the US describe as "an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia who has coordinated attacks for the RIS network".
Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, are the other two defendants.
The pair are accused of recruiting or attempting to recruit US-based individuals to "surveil and attempt to murder a prominent US-based Russian dissident".
The FBI's James Barnacle said the group "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".
One of the incidents is as recent as this summer. The DoJ described how the RIS network was able to recruit someone in the US to surveil and eventually murder a Russian dissident in the US.
Suarez allegedly sent the recruit to two locations linked to the victim with "explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance". In exchange, the recruit was offered between $1,000 (Â£743) and $1,500.
Suarez and Castro are said to have offered an additional $40,000 if the US resident could "eliminate" the dissident.
The DoJ said the RIS recruit did not go through with it, which led Suarez to try and recruit "multiple other individuals within the United States". He allegedly offered "substantial sums of money to carry out the targeting of US based victims".
The release by the DoJ goes on to list other instances in which the accused allegedly tried to recruit others to kill those who were a perceived threat to Russia.
It said that in 2025, Khrameev junior allegedly recruited a US citizen to surveil and murder someone in Lithuania who was "telling lies about Russia". The release quotes Khrameev as saying the purpose was to target "all the countries that are helping Ukraine".
His father, Khrameev senior, is said to have offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the individual in Lithuania for "spreading dirt about my country" and "distorting history".
Khrameev senior, Suarez and Castro are the only ones also charged with "participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire". If found guilty, this charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence.
It is not the first time authorities thwart threats of this kind.
Last month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained an individual allegedly working for the Kremlin and who was plotting to murder an American-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw.
Tusk told reporters the American-Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime", adding: "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons."
In 2024, German authorities were reportedly warned by US intelligence of a Russian plot to kill Armin Papperger, the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall.
Moscow dismissed the accusation at the time, with Kremlin spokesman Peskov saying: "It's all presented in the style of another fake story, so such reports cannot be taken seriously."
The fresh accusations from the DoJ come at a time of closer relations between Moscow and Washington following US President Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025.
A few weeks ago, the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) visited Moscow for talks with figures from Russia's intelligence services - an unconventional move that led to speculation.
The Kremlin confirmed that talks between John Ratcliffe and the intelligence services had taken place. President Trump did not say what was discussed but described the meeting as "semi-routine".

Davidâs view
If you donât appreciate how quickly Democrats are entering attack mode against AI, just count the groups theyâve started since our last edition alone.
Thereâs Tomorrow Together, the new PAC formed by veterans of the Bernie Sanders and Kamala Harris campaigns, working to make theirs âthe party that wins on AI.â Thereâs Who Decides, launched by New York state legislator Alex Bores in the wake of his failed House bid, which became a proxy war between AI industry PACs.
Joining the list today: The Stop Bleeding the Future pledge. Developed by an array of progressive groups, it commits candidates to ârefuse all money fromâ the most active AI industry PAC and to âcondemn its efforts to stop commonsense AI laws.â Its first signatories include Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, who had warned for months that the party needed AI policies that werenât written by the companies.
QuitGPT, the coalition that wrote the pledge, began circulating it in May. âWe want to make them irrelevant and toxic,â Michael Baick, one of its organizers, said when we talked yesterday. âWe want any politician or staffer who gets an email from these guys to think: This is bleeding the future.â
They might not need much pushing. In the year since I covered voter anger at data center construction in Virginia, AI angst has moved from the political frontiers to center stage. I spent most of Tuesday at the Pro-Human Assembly, where Steve Bannon and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., anchored a day of nervous programming about the dangers of AI and the need for âguardrailsâ built by an accountable government.
âI donât think a pledge should be limited to [the Leading the Future AI industry PAC], because theyâre already finding ways to shift their money,â Bores told me. âBut theyâre toxic to this debate.â
Leading the Future chose not to comment on the âbleedingâ pledge. Below the surface, there is a lot of contemptuous finger-pointing about where the anti-AI energy now coursing through the political-media landscape is coming from. Whatâs the role of Effective Altruism, and that movementâs money, in fueling âdoomerismâ that will advantage one company at the expense of another?
But weâre in the middle of an election, with ballots in the mail, and the Democratic Partyâs conversation about this is pretty simple. They see a president who isnât popular, an industry thatâs less popular, and â when those are combined â a very straightforward story about wealthy job-destroyers using their political access to put everybody at risk.
âI say to them that if you believe in democracy, if you believe that the people have a right to determine their future, stop pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into super PACs,â Sanders said at the conference.
Sanders was one of the first left-wing politicians to understand the backlash against data centers. The topic came up during his âFight Oligarchyâ tours. He polled audiences on what was happening in their towns and what was making them anxious. The answer, quite often, was AI.
There are some Democratic skeptics of Sandersâ approach here, and his own thinking about the world-ending danger of AI â an idea that is pushed hard by Effective Altruists. But I am starting to see wide adoption of his people-versus-Silicon Valley approach.
I expect to see more after Tuesday, when Senate Democrats sank the Clarity Act, the top priority of the cryptocurrency industry for the last two years, without much worry about the consequences.
Republicans could resurrect the bill after the midterms, but itâs not likely after a failure this big. The crypto industry spent more than $130 million on the 2024 elections to put friendly politicians in office, from both parties â out of necessity, because the filibuster wasnât likely to get busted for their bill.
Democrats like Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., got help from the PACs, on the expectation that theyâd be amenable to collaboration if they won their 2024 races.
But the dynamics shifted quickly. The president and his family had made more than $1 billion from crypto. How could Democrats go home and tell their voters that theyâd enriched the president on behalf of an industry that funded their campaigns? Gallego, speaking for a lot of Democrats, decided that Republicans care âmore about making sure the president keeps making money than actually bringing regulations.â
The anti-AI push comes from the same thinking. The president can be counted on to denounce AI regulation. That makes it easier to run against when heâs unpopular, and impossible to support when Democrats want to win their own primaries.
âThe industry still thinks soft dollars will buy them love, in part because of the mistaken belief that the crypto playbook is repeatable,â said Sam Silverman, a Democratic strategist advising candidates on AI messaging. âItâs not. Voters donât give a f*ck about crypto. When AI is the defining topic of the election, do you think taking millions from Marc Andreessen, Greg Brockman, and Joe Lonsdale will be palatable to the base?â
Room for Disagreement
Across the aisle, the presidentâs party is more divided over AI than it was over crypto. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who got flattened by Trump when he ran for president, was also early to data center skepticism, and keeps warning Republicans that they donât want to be identified as reflexively pro-AI.
âIf they say, âHey, we protected you against rate increases, we made sure local communities would be able to choose what type of, if any, they want in terms of construction, and then we want to have an AI bill of rights,â thatâs where you get huge majorities,â he said this week.

AUSTIN, Texas—A chair with Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian’s name on it sat empty Tuesday in the hearing room of the Texas House Committee on Energy Resources.
Committee Chairman Drew Darby had called Christian to testify before the panel, which oversees the Railroad Commission, regulator of the state’s powerful oil and gas industry. Christian failed to appear before the committee and wrote in a letter that he had a scheduling conflict.
Darby, a Republican from San Angelo, opened the committee meeting with stern words for the commissioner.
“I do not recall my request for his presence as being optional,” he said. “It is beyond clear that Commissioner Christian has willfully chosen to defy this committee.”
Disagreement over a change in the Railroad Commission’s public participation policy threatens to spill over into a larger dispute between the oversight committee and the oil and gas overseer, whose three members are elected statewide.
The tensions come as Texas faces a growing backlog of abandoned oil and gas wells it’s on the hook to plug, and large volumes of oilfield wastewater injected underground are causing blowouts and leaks. Meanwhile, Republican Bo French and Democrat Jon Rosenthal are locked in an unusually close race for a seat on the Railroad Commission.
Christian has doubled down on the new public participation policy that he introduced last month at a commission meeting, as first reported by Inside Climate News. The new policy increases the frequency of listening sessions but leaves it to the discretion of the commissioners whether there will be a public comment period at each meeting, which previously had been standard. Darby had criticized the new policy and called on Christian to testify.
In written testimony provided to the House committee, Christian wrote that the policy should be judged by its results over time. He also called out the nonprofit Commission Shift, which advocates for reforms to oil and gas oversight in Texas, for accepting funding from national foundations that support climate activism.
Also on Tuesday, before the committee’s hearing, the Railroad Commission hosted an open meeting, the first since the policy change last month. The room was packed with residents who had traveled hundreds of miles from Southeast Texas and the Permian Basin to give comments to the elected officials leading the agency.
Christian and the commission’s other two elected members chose, under the new public participation policy, to add an agenda item for public comment. They also heard public comments regarding an ExxonMobil carbon capture and sequestration permit in Jefferson County before voting on it.
When it was the turn of Virginia Palacios, executive director of Commission Shift, to provide public comment, she reiterated that residents need opportunities to speak directly to the elected commissioners.
Christian began grilling Palacios, accusing her of presenting a “false premise” to state legislators when speaking out against the new policy.
“How dare you come here,” he told Palacios. “You can’t come here today and do anything but bitch some more.
He added, “You ain’t in it for the good of the people, you’re in it for stirring up stink.”
When Palacios tried to respond, Chairman Christi Craddick cut her off, saying her allotted three minutes was over.
“Your time is now up,” Craddick said. “We’ll be happy to escort you out, but I happen to agree with Commissioner Christian.”
“It was difficult to watch an elected official act in such an unprofessional manner,” Commission Shift later wrote in a blog post.
“Commissioner Christian believes that his written testimony speaks for itself,” his staff wrote in response to questions from Inside Climate News.
Not long after, the House Committee on Energy Resources heard testimony on the Railroad Commission. While Christian was a no-show, Craddick appeared to testify on orphan well plugging and inactive wells.
Several individuals gave testimony on the importance of public input at the Railroad Commission.
